bullets: The 2026 midterms cemented a Democratic House and Senate majority, forcing GOP leaders to confront internal fractures and a costly war in Iran that threatens 2028 prospects (The Bulwark, Zeteo).

Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff has intensified hard‑line immigration and anti‑immigrant rhetoric, polarizing Congress and prompting calls for impeachment of officials like Pete Hegseth (Bulwark Takes, Here Be Dragons).

Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang scandal—an alleged affair with a Chinese spy—has exposed deep U.S. tech vulnerabilities, prompting bipartisan warnings that the administration ignored security red flags (JVL, Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger).
Democratic strategists warn that despite the “Blue Wave,” the party’s infrastructure and funding gaps risk losing momentum in 2028, urging a focus on building state‑level capacity (Lauren Egan).
The GOP’s $400 million spending advantage failed to translate into seats, highlighting inefficiencies in media buys and the need for a new campaign narrative (Dan Pfeiffer).

Health‑care reform remains a flashpoint, with Senator Bernie Sanders pushing Medicare‑for‑All while moderates threaten to derail progress, risking a repeat of the 2020 intra‑party split (Jonathan Cohn).

items.subject: The Blue Wave Didn’t End the Gerrymandering Arms Race
bullets: Rep. Henry Cuellar (D‑TX) won re‑election after 2025 GOP‑drawn maps, intended to favor Republicans, backfired and made his district more Democratic, prompting his sarcastic thanks to the speaker and White House.

The 2025 Republican redistricting push, spurred by Trump, led to unexpectedly competitive districts nationwide, contributing to a massive Democratic House majority and prompting Democrats to consider adopting GOP gerrymandering tactics.

Wisconsin Gov‑elect David Crowley announced plans to order a new map favoring Democrats, while Democrats in Virginia, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland are also moving to redraw maps before the next cycle, though some moderates urge non‑partisan standards.

items.subject: Sex Crimes, Lies, War, Money: MAGA’s 2026 ‘Self-Immolation’ Keeps Getting Worse
bullets: After the 2026 midterms, Trump and GOP leaders admit the party is demoralized, with internal feuding erupting publicly and fears the ongoing Iran war will cripple Republican prospects for 2028.
Pollster John McLaughlin warned Republicans have forgotten the 2024 winning formula and need rebuilding, while a senior administration official described MAGA as having ‘self‑immolated.’
Vice President JD Vance privately warned the Iran conflict will destroy the party unless it ends quickly, echoing widespread alarm among GOP operatives.

items.subject: Spies Like Trump
bullets: The newsletter alleges that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was caught in a Chinese MSS honeypot, that members of the Trump administration—and Trump himself—knew and invited him onto Air Force One to facilitate chip sales to China.
It claims Trump personally approved Huang’s request to sell Nvidia chips to China, framing the episode as evidence of Trump being a massive national‑security threat and possibly a foreign agent.

items.subject: College Republicans Revolt Against Trump
bullets: The College Republican Patriot Coalition, representing chapters at universities such as Illinois, Florida, Virginia, Maryland, Georgia and New York, issued an open letter blaming Trump for abandoning MAGA principles, breaking campaign promises and driving the GOP toward a “cliff.”

The letter calls for a purge of the Trump administration and a new champion, citing grievances that include Israel policy, which they claim pushed Trump into an Iran war, and hints at possible ties to white‑nationalist podcaster Nick Fuentes.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Musical Chairs on the MAGA Titanic
bullets: Nvidia ousted CEO Jensen Huang immediately after a board‑announced probe into an alleged affair with a Chinese spy, while China’s Ministry of State Security has not responded.

Mike Pence framed the 2024 midterm losses as a rejection of GOP economic populism and urged a return to traditional conservative principles, but his vision clashes with the New Right’s Trump‑aligned agenda.

New Right group American Ascent, funded with $12 million by donor Tom Klingenstein, seeks to recruit next‑generation national‑conservative Republicans, positioning itself as both Trump’s heir and a generational shift despite the party’s internal factional turmoil.

items.newsletter: Paul Krugman and Heather Cox Richardson from Paul Krugman
items.subject: Paul Krugman and Heather Cox Richardson in Conversation | CUNY Graduate Center
bullets: A live video conversation between Paul Krugman and Heather Cox Richardson, beginning at minute 34, is available for viewers to watch on the CUNY Graduate Center platform.

items.subject: Is Ayanna Pressley About to Challenge Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker?
bullets: Mississippi elected Democrat Scott Colom, ending a decades‑long GOP hold and giving Democrats 55 Senate seats, with Alaska still undecided.
A Change.org petition urging “Make Ayanna Pressley the Speaker of the House” has gathered about 30,000 signatures, signaling growing progressive push against minority leader Hakeem Jeffries.
The newsletter highlights the petition as a potential early sign of a challenge to Jeffries for the Democratic House speaker role.

items.subject: Climates of Treason
bullets: Krugman argues that Trump’s administration deliberately buried the Nvidia‑Huang security scandal, exposing a broader pattern of ideological and financial betrayals that weaken U.S. national security and its tech edge against China.

He claims MAGA officials, including Trump and allies, favor authoritarian models like Putin’s for ideological reasons while exploiting China‑related deals for personal profit, citing Nvidia’s $25 million Trump fundraiser and hundreds of millions funneled from the AI industry.

Krugman contends that this incompetence and self‑interest have led to lost wars with Iran and China, a collapsing global reputation, and a government that is unpatriotic and unwilling to sacrifice for the nation.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: How Republicans Are Choosing to Lose Again
bullets: Republics lost the 2026 midterms by nearly 14 points in the popular vote, falling short of 56 Senate seats and about 260 House seats, even losing traditionally red states like Kansas, South Carolina, Texas, and Mississippi.

After the loss, Trump fired campaign chief Susie Wiles and installed Stephen Miller, while House Republicans elected Jim Jordan as minority leader, signaling a continued hard‑right strategy rather than a post‑defeat recalibration.
Pfeiffer argues this leadership shift shows the GOP is denying the election reality and is poised to repeat the same losing approach in the 2028 cycle.

items.subject: Vivek Ramaswamy Took Such a Beating That He Disappeared (w/ Nick Wright & Anderson Clayton)
bullets: Tim Miller argues that many 2024 voters initially backed the Republican “bully” party but turned away after seeing harsh ICE policies and attempts to restrict voting rights

Nick Wright notes a growing recognition in the manosphere that overt meanness isn’t strength, while also criticizing sports commentators pandering to MAGA and lamenting his own mis‑call on Nikola Jokić
Tim calls for patience in the lame‑duck period and interviews young NC Democratic chair Anderson Clayton about the party’s surprising recent victories in the state

items.subject: One Easy Trick for Dems to Maintain Their Blue-Wave Gains
bullets: Democratic operatives warn that despite recent midterm gains in traditionally red states like Texas and South Carolina, state parties lack infrastructure and funding, risking missed opportunities in the 2028 election cycle.

DNC chair Ken Martin’s fifty‑state program now gives $1 million monthly to state parties, but fundraising shortfalls and recent staff layoffs raise doubts about sustaining long‑term investment in red‑state organization.

Leaders such as Sen. Raphael Warnock and former DNC chair Jaime Harrison urge presidential candidates to commit resources to voter registration, recruitment, and building durable state‑level organizations, proposing a 57‑state pledge to centralize effort.

items.subject: Laura Loomer’s MAGA Pay-for-Play Feud Takes a Very Suspicious Turn | MAGA Wednesdays
bullets: Sam Stein and Will Sommer host a special MAGA Wednesdays episode featuring a neo-Nazi leader who accidentally livestreamed a sex act, Mark Levin's public AOL account meltdown, and a lawsuit alleging foreign money and luxury gifts in Trump’s circle.
The episode also reports James Fishback receiving a $4 million judgment and Vivek Ramaswamy’s disappearance from Twitter, while MAGA media prepares to name a Citizen Journalist of the Year.

items.newsletter: Here Be Dragons from Barbara F. Walter
items.subject: I’m Thrilled Stephen Miller Is Chief of Staff
bullets: Stephen Miller’s appointment as White House Chief of Staff is seen as a strategic move by Trump to give Democrats a common enemy, forcing them to unite against his hard‑right agenda.

Miller’s uncompromising stance on mass deportations, anti‑immigrant policies and ending birthright citizenship will polarize Congress, prompting Democrats to rally quickly or risk being blamed for supporting these measures in 2028.

Political scientists Diana Evans and Berker Kavasoglu suggest that a strong opposition party is less likely to cooperate when ideologically distant, implying Miller will intensify partisan gridlock and force Democrats to sharpen their opposition tactics.

items.subject: Stephen Miller Is Still Trump’s Daddy on Immigration
bullets: Donald Trump, in a 60 Minutes interview, praised his party’s immigration enforcement but admitted the removal of some lawful workers, hinting a bipartisan deal could be “doable” in the next Congress, yet reversed this stance a day later, denying any amnesty and insisting his policy had not changed.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin echoed Trump’s claim that Democrats were reaching out for an immigration deal, suggested a DACA‑focused compromise, but mistakenly conflated “citizen” with “legal permanent resident” and insisted no amnesty could result, reflecting confusion within the administration.

items.subject: Destroy All Monsters
bullets: Trump, now backed by Stephen Miller and rallying behind Pete Hegseth, is actively fighting to retain control of the Republican Party and is using the Iran war as a political weapon against JD Vance.

The newsletter warns Democrats that their sole priority for the next two years should be to destroy Trump’s political standing, as he shows no signs of stepping aside and is willing to let the GOP lose ground to remain the party’s focal point.

JD Vance’s recent criticism of Trump’s war strategy has been turned against him by Trump, who framed a media question that forces Vance to publicly reaffirm support for the Iran war, limiting Vance’s options.

items.subject: ‘The Future Is F*ck You Politics’ – Jennifer Welch and Mehdi on the Midterms, Schumer & Jeffries, and… Charlie Kirk
bullets: Jennifer Welch and Mehdi analyze the 2026 midterm ‘Blue Wave’, debating whether Senate leaders Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries should be removed and mocking Ted Cruz as Texas’s sole remaining Republican elected official

items.subject: How Dems Can Avoid Another Self-Destructive Health Care Fight
bullets: Senator Bernie Sanders is urging Democrats to use their new majorities, secured on Tuesday, to pass Medicare for All legislation quickly, while senators‑elect like Adam Hamilton of Kansas publicly oppose the plan.

The piece warns that a repeat of the 2020 intra‑party fight—where Medicare for All became an all‑or‑nothing litmus test—could derail health‑care reform as rising costs and Republican Medicaid cuts threaten coverage for millions.
It argues Democrats should avoid a self‑destructive split by finding a compromise path that expands coverage without the polarizing, single‑track approach championed by Sanders.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Trump’s Chipghazi
bullets: The New York Times reported that in May, Marco Rubio told President Trump on Air Force One that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was involved with a Chinese spy, a claim Trump allegedly ignored while continuing to consult Huang.

Politico and the Financial Times revealed that Commerce Department officials, led by Howard Lutnick, ignored dozens of warnings about Nvidia’s advanced chips being diverted to China and failed to place spy‑linked firm Megaspeed on the entity list despite $4.8 billion in chip sales.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer condemned Trump for knowing about Huang’s alleged espionage ties for over a year and doing nothing, while bipartisan congressional investigations are now promised to probe the scandal.

items.subject: Live Event with Heather Cox Richardson
bullets: A live event with historian Heather Cox Richardson will stream on both Substack platforms, with a Zoom registration link provided.

Krugman promotes his new ebook, Navigating the Chaos, summarizing the past two years and outlining Democratic priorities for a lasting progressive movement, available on Amazon, Kobo, Bookshop, and Nook.

items.subject: Cat-Scratch Fervo
bullets: A University of Florida study shows most tech IPOs now lose money, highlighting a decline in IPO quality as banks push risky deals despite abundant private capital.
Fervo Energy, a geothermal startup that went public in May 2026 raising over $2 billion, saw its share price plunge 70% below IPO price after a short‑seller report, then jump 25% on Q3 earnings.
The author questions whether Fervo’s ambitious goal of 1 GW by 2030 will revolutionize clean energy or prove to be an overhyped, truth‑bending promotion.

items.newsletter: Tim, Sarah and JVL - The Bulwark
items.subject: Republicans Lost So Badly They’re Now Fighting Over Who to Blame
bullets: Tim, Sarah and JVL dissect the post‑election GOP fallout, noting Stephen Miller’s appointment as White House chief of staff and Jim Jordan’s rise to House minority leader while criticizing Axios’s claim the system held against Trump interference.”,

items.subject: How Trump’s Top Tech Ally Got Caught in a Honey Trap
bullets: Marc Polymeropoulos, a 26‑year CIA veteran, and Michael Weiss detail alleged Chinese honey‑trap that seduced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, risking exposure of U.S. AI secrets.
U.S. intelligence reportedly uncovered the plot, Marco Rubio warned the White House, yet the Trump administration, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, appears reluctant to act.

items.subject: The Dems Won Big. Now What Do They Do?
bullets: Democrats swept the 2026 midterms, crushing Trump’s MAGA movement and securing large majorities in both the House and Senate, reshaping the presidential map.

The new Congress faces pressure to address affordability issues and hold Trump accountable while internal left and center-left factions debate the party’s 21st‑century identity ahead of the 2028 nomination race.
A note that the usual ‘First Draft’ newsletter will skip Wednesday for Veterans Day and return Thursday.

items.subject: Stephen Miller Is a Problem
bullets: Donald Trump named Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, prompting warnings from GOP senators like Thom Tillis that Miller’s racist, hard‑line agenda will intensify the administration’s combative policies

Senators Mike Rounds, James Lankford and Bernie Moreno defended Miller, arguing the president need not seek Senate approval and that Miller’s “smart and tough” approach signals a readiness for political war
The bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus, once 43 members, now faces collapse after the midterms, with only seven Republicans expected to remain versus nineteen Democrats in the 120th Congress

items.subject: The Dark Lesson From the Midterms
bullets: The midterm results showed voters explicitly rejecting promises to lower prices, end wars, and curb corruption, demanding politicians stop making empty claims and focus on real policy outcomes.

Despite widespread criticism of democracy’s fragility, the author argues that American institutions—courts, press, and electoral processes—continued to function effectively, proving the system’s resilience.
The piece warns that unchallenged optimism about the past decade’s stability risks normalizing authoritarian tendencies and undermines vigilance against political erosion.

items.subject: Jensen Huang’s Affair Isn’t the Only Reason the U.S. Is Losing Ground to China in the Tech War
bullets: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence suspects of commercial espionage for China, sparking concerns over insider threats in U.S. tech firms.

The scandal exposes deeper vulnerabilities in U.S. economic dominance, highlighting how personal misconduct can intersect with national security risks and China's broader strategy to undermine American technological leadership.

items.subject: Why save the media?
bullets: Hamish argues that saving the media means preserving its core function of scaling trust and understanding through stories, which has been eroded by the attention economy over the past decade.
He cites a 2006 Dominion Post piece on WWII veterans planning a Crete trip, whose personal impact on veterans’ families illustrates how even brief local stories can profoundly matter.
The author frames journalism as community‑service: by sharing geographically constrained narratives, media enables people to communicate, shape collective identity, and solve problems together.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: The Wannabe Fascist Has Lost His Fastball
bullets: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth angrily defends himself at the Pentagon against impeachment, prompting a live‑stream analysis by Lt. Gen. Mark Hertling and Ben Parler on Substack and YouTube at 9:30 a.m. EST.

Donald Trump, after appointing Stephen Miller as chief of staff, remains in a state of “nostalgic” distraction, issuing election denial posts, hosting bizarre press conferences with UFC CEO Dana White, and appearing on a surprise CSPAN call‑in, signaling a dysfunctional White House and a lack of decisive action.

Trump’s National Security Council issued a classified memo warning that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is linked to Chinese spy Alice Huang, yet Trump invited Huang onto a presidential trip to China in May and continues to host him at the White House despite the intelligence warning, exposing a national‑security scandal involving the president.

items.subject: Announcing NEXT
bullets: Pete Buttigieg announces his new book NEXT, set to release on January 26, 2027, arguing for systemic change beyond party politics after the 2026 election shift.
The book will outline how to build a better America, offering principles rather than policy details, and is available for pre-order at local booksellers and major audiobook platforms.

items.subject: Run, Chris, Run!
bullets: Chris Van Hollen is positioned to replace Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader, citing Schumer’s low approval and history of backing Republicans and Israel’s policies, while Van Hollen’s support for progressive mayor Zohran Mamdani and activism abroad is highlighted as a contrast.
Neera Tanden, chief of a liberal think tank, urges Democratic activists not to demand special favors from the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress, warning that such requests could backfire.
Pete Hegseth faces potential impeachment this week, with the article noting the possibility of formal proceedings against the conservative commentator.

items.subject: The Cyberpunking of America (Fixed)
bullets: Tesla is ending production of the Cybertruck, which critics described as a “mechanical cockroach” and a “culture war on wheels” that shifted from eco‑status symbol to MAGA signal over its seven‑year run.

Krugman links the Cybertruck’s failure and Zuckerberg’s $80 billion Metaverse loss to a broader cyberpunk‑inspired mindset among tech billionaires, who view dystopian futures as manifestos rather than warnings.
He warns that despite these tech elites’ grandiose visions, public opposition to data centers, AI, and such dystopian projects remains strong and could curb the ‘cyberpunking’ of America.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Republicans Outspent Democrats by $400 Million. Why Did They Still Lose?
bullets: Republicans outspent Democrats by over $400 million across the 2026 cycle, with Elon Musk contributing more than $400 million—including $200 million for Texas candidate Ken Paxton, who lost by double digits.]

Despite the spending advantage, Democrats won due to favorable polls, candidate quality, and the inefficiency of $11 billion in TV ads, which struggle to reach persuadable voters as cord‑cutting rises.

items.subject: The Cyberpunking of America
bullets: Tesla is ending production of the Cybertruck, which the New York Times called a “mechanical cockroach” and a “culture war on wheels” after a seven‑year rise and fall tied to Elon Musk’s shifting public image.”,

items.subject: Measles elimination decision brewing, where is the fall vaccination data, and good news you might have missed
bullets: A secret panel of eight experts will decide by Nov 16 if the U.S. has lost measles elimination status after a continuous 12‑month spread of the same genotype, likely leading to an endemic label and higher disease burden.

National ILI rates are at 2.8% (just below the 2.9% sick‑season trigger), with the South and West at 3.3%; flu positivity is 9% and three child deaths have occurred this season, while CDC has not released fall vaccination rates, raising accountability concerns.

items.subject: I Worked at the Pentagon. Congress Must Impeach and Remove Pete Hegseth Now
bullets: The author cites a recent video where Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth threatened to use the U.S. military against “radical Democrats,” calling it evidence of violent extremism and psychological instability deserving impeachment.

He recounts whistleblowing on Hegseth’s illegal dismantling of the Pentagon’s civilian protection center and warns that his far‑right ideology is turning the U.S. into a fascist, globally domineering power.

items.subject: Trump’s End Could Come Sooner Than Anyone Thinks (w/ Mark Blumberg) | Psycho Politics
bullets: Conway warns that a politically weakened Trump, bolstered by Stephen Miller's rising influence, may pursue revenge-driven actions that could be more dangerous than before.

He and former federal prosecutor Mark Blumberg discuss the Rule of Law Project, which unites ex-DOJ lawyers, FBI agents, journalists, and whistleblowers to build criminal cases against Trump administration officials.

items.subject: Neo-Nazi Leader Accidentally Livestreams Masturbation Session
bullets: Neo‑Nazi influencer Christopher Pohlhaus, known as “Hammer,” streamed a World of Warcraft session on Kick that unintentionally continued while he engaged in a two‑and‑a‑half hour cyber‑sex call with a woman using the screen name “Iron Maiden 14,” exposing the act to about fifteen viewers.

The incident, which occurred on the night of the midterm results on Tuesday, highlighted the hypocrisy of a white‑supremacist leader promoting “traditional values” while publicly masturbating, prompting horrified comments from viewers.

items.subject: BREAKING: Trump Hosts Ridiculous Press Conference with UFC CEO Dana White
bullets: Trump held an impromptu press conference where he evaded questions about a Chinese spy allegedly linked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and rejected any softening of his immigration crackdown.
When pressed about Putin and commentator Pete Hegseth, Trump lashed out at reporters, displaying increasing hostility toward the press.
Trump attempted to recruit UFC CEO Dana White as his press secretary, but White rebuffed the offer, highlighting the awkwardness of the exchange.

items.subject: Do Democrats Actually Have an ‘Affordability’ Agenda – or a Plan to Pass It?
bullets: Democrats won a decisive midterm mandate, with 75% of voters rating the economy negatively and 59% citing gas, groceries, and healthcare costs as major concerns, yet the party’s “affordability” agenda remains vague and largely a return to pre‑Trump policies.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other moderates promise to reverse Trump’s healthcare cuts—ending Medicaid reductions, reauthorizing Obamacare subsidies, and stopping tariff‑driven gas price hikes—yet offer no substantive plan to lower overall healthcare costs or guarantee coverage for all Americans.

Progressive voices like Rep.-elect Melat Kiros criticize the current agenda as insufficient, noting that 61% of voters want a larger government role in healthcare, but Democrats have yet to present concrete measures beyond policy reversals to make healthcare truly affordable.

items.subject: Trump’s Interview Sends MAGA Into a Full-Blown Meltdown | MAGA Mondays
bullets: Will Sommer and Sam Stein report that Trump's post‑midterm interview, in which he floated an immigration deal with Democrats and claimed the elections were stolen, has sparked outrage among hard‑liners like Megyn Kelly and The Blaze, exposing fissures in the MAGA coalition.

The piece also highlights scrutiny of Laura Loomer's paid political posts, Russell Brand's prison sentence raising doubts about MAGA's tolerance of alleged predators, and escalating infighting over corruption allegations within Trump's White House.

items.subject: Defund WAR!
bullets: The author urges Democrats, who now hold a historic mandate, to act immediately in Congress to end the Iran war, arguing it would curb inflation and price pressures.
He claims Democrats can force President Trump’s hand by using three legislative tools to compel a cease‑fire, without needing to sway public opinion, since Americans already oppose the conflict.

items.subject: Palestinian Suffering Was ‘Never Guiding’ Biden’s Gaza Policy, New Book Says
bullets: Akbar Shahid Ahmed’s new book, based on interviews with over 150 officials, argues Biden knew of Palestinian and Lebanese suffering during the Gaza war but let it not shape U.S. policy.

According to Ahmed, senior staff like Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk and National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan dismissed reports of Gaza starvation, claiming Palestinians ‘don’t look skinny in the photographs.’
The book also reveals a Biden aide who halted criticism of Russia solely to maintain U.S. support for Israel, a detail Ahmed describes as ‘insane.’

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: It’s Not a Pivot. It’s a Performance.
bullets: Trump promoted Stephen Miller to chief of staff and hinted at a softer immigration stance to appease business interests, but dismissed any genuine empathy for migrants and doubted Democrats would drop investigations into his corruption.
In the 60 Minutes interview, Trump insisted he will never forgive his political enemies, reinforcing his unchanged hard‑line persona despite recent electoral setbacks.

Democrat Scott Colom is poised to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, leading incumbent Cindy Hyde‑Smith by about 0.3% and winning roughly a quarter of the white vote, including strong support from younger white voters.

items.subject: 🐊 ‘Didn’t Even Try’: How Chuck Schumer and Dem Elites Lost Florida
bullets: Democrats celebrated sweeping midterm wins but suffered a notable loss in Florida, where GOP candidates Byron Donalds and Ashley Moody narrowly beat Democrats David Jolly and Angie Nixon, exposing vulnerability despite holding the state.
Strategists and pollsters on both sides say the Florida races were far tighter than expected, with the GOP fearing a deeper Democratic surge that could threaten their dominance in the Sunshine State.
Trump’s weekend speculation about appointing UFC CEO Dana White as press secretary added a farcical distraction amid the serious post‑election analysis.

items.subject: The Texas Miracle
bullets: Texas Democrats swept every statewide office in the 2026 midterms, with Gov. Gina Hinojosa winning by 7 points despite gerrymandered congressional districts that still favor Republicans.

The blue shift was driven by a dramatic leftward swing among Latino voters, who rejected Trump’s anti‑immigrant policies and ICE raids, suggesting a potentially lasting realignment similar to California’s post‑1994 shift.
If Texas remains reliably Democratic, its outsized influence on national issues—like textbook standards via the Texas Board of Education—could reshape U.S. politics and curb authoritarian trends.

items.newsletter: Sam Stein & Tim Miller @ The Bulwark
items.subject: Todd Blanche’s CNN Interview Could Come Back to Bite Him
bullets: Todd Blanche appeared on CNN defending Trump’s threats to imprison Democrats, denying allegations against Susie Wiles, and pledging to shield Stephen Miller from congressional probes.
Will Saletan and Catherine Rampell argue that Blanche’s attempts to preempt investigations actually furnish Democrats with additional grounds to launch inquiries into his actions.

items.subject: Dems Won Big. Naturally, They’re Fighting About It.
bullets: Democrats won big in the midterms, with candidates like Roy Cooper (won by 20 points), Abdul El‑Sayed, Jamie Ager, Randy Villegas, James Talarico and Annie Andrews securing victories by blending economic populism and cultural moderation.

Despite the wins, party operatives quickly resumed factional fights over issues such as Israel, Medicare for All, and campaign strategy, a pattern the author says reflects entrenched, dopamine‑driven infighting.

Strategists note the success came from a historic populist vein—heavy on economic concerns, light on culture—mirroring Sanders‑era and Clinton‑era Democrats, and warn that renewed infighting risks disconnecting from voters.

items.subject: Author of IHRA Antisemitism Definition Tells Zeteo It’s ‘So Poisoned I Wouldn’t Use It’
bullets: Kenneth Stern, lead drafter of the IHRA antisemitism definition, told Zeteo UK the definition is “so poisoned I wouldn’t use it,” warning it could increase antisemitism and silence Palestine discussion in schools.

Stern argues the definition, never meant for education, encourages groupthink and makes teachers fearful of teaching about Israel‑Palestine, contrary to Sir David Bell’s recommendation that schools adopt it.
Despite the government’s immediate acceptance of Bell’s 27‑point report urging IHRA adoption, Stern says the policy will deter critical thinking and harm free debate on the issue.

items.subject: Republicans Have a Choice to Make After Trump’s Crushing Defeat (w/ Mike Murphy) | Bulwark on Sunday
bullets: Bill Kristol and Mike Murphy argue that Trump’s midterm loss could push Republicans toward a post‑Trump realignment, citing internal chaos like Stephen Miller’s growing influence and Pete Hegseth’s precarious position.
They warn of a potential Nixon‑style collapse of the party’s leadership, suggesting the GOP must confront its dependence on Trump to avoid further electoral damage.
Looking ahead to 2028, they contend JD Vance faces a far tougher path than expected, given the lingering fallout from Trump’s dominance and the party’s internal fractures.

items.subject: Reminder: 20% OFF Bulwark+ Ends Tonight
bullets: The Bulwark offers a 20% flash sale on Bulwark+ subscriptions, ending tonight at midnight.
The newsletter frames the midterm Democratic win as the start of a longer fight against MAGA and Trumpism, urging readers to join their mission.
Support from members, not billionaires, funds their investigative reporting and liberal advocacy over the next two years.

items.newsletter: Sam Stein & Tim Miller @ The Bulwark
items.subject: Picking the Biggest 2026 GOP Loser Is Harder Than You Think
bullets: Tim Miller and Sam Stein create a fantasy draft ranking the biggest Republican failures of 2026, highlighting defeats of figures like Vivek Ramaswamy and Ken Paxton.
The Bulwark promotes a 20% flash sale on its subscription service, emphasizing its commitment to liberal reporting and accountability while offering the draft as entertaining analysis.

items.subject: Can Chuck Schumer Be Stopped? Mehdi Talks to Commentator and Socialist Emma Vigeland
bullets: Emma Vigeland says progressives should oust Senate leader Chuck Schumer and House leader Hakeem Jeffries, blaming Schomer for enabling fascism and failing to back progressive candidates like Angie Nixon’s Florida Senate run
The interview argues that Democratic establishment’s support acts as a ‘jet pack’ for candidates, and discusses whether AOC should run for president in 2028
The episode is freely available and invites listeners to become paid subscribers or donate to support the newsletter’s independent journalism

items.subject: We Convened a Group of Committed GOP Voters to See How They’re Coping
bullets: A focus group of voters who supported Trump in 2020, 2024 and most 2024 midterms blamed the Republican establishment, not Trump, for the party’s defeat.
Participants said GOP leaders failed to communicate policy successes and alienated the base, citing a lack of clear messaging and internal infighting.
They expressed frustration that the party prioritized culture wars over economic issues, believing this cost them broader electoral appeal.

items.subject: On Capacity
bullets: The article argues that modern cultural praxis for self‑improvement is broken, especially for disciplined, long‑term goals that require “doing the wise thing,” leading to chronic failure despite motivation.

Horton links this failure to mismatched beliefs and lack of reliable cultural tools, noting that even well‑studied problems like procrastination remain unsolved across domains such as health, finance, and infrastructure.
He suggests the core challenge is creating systems that help people reliably achieve major behavioral changes, rather than blaming individuals or relying on vague policy fixes.

items.subject: After the Bubble Bursts
bullets: AI capital spending, especially on data centers, has surged but investors now face a “Wile E. Coyote” risk as hyperscaler stocks have fallen 27% and AI‑bond insurance costs have spiked, hinting a possible bubble burst.
Krugman argues that if the AI bubble bursts, it will likely trigger a recession deeper than the late‑1990s tech slump, with a slow recovery and elevated unemployment lasting years.
He will later outline historical recession patterns, why post‑bubble recoveries are sluggish, compare an AI bust to the dot‑com crash, and argue policy responses will be insufficient.

items.subject: Stephen Miller May Now Be the De Facto President
bullets: Bill Kristol and former Trump aide Sarah Matthews argue that after the GOP’s midterm loss, Trump may elevate Stephen Miller to run the White House, effectively making him the de facto president.

They warn Miller’s appointment would shift internal power dynamics, concentrating policy control in his hands and marginalizing traditional officials like Pete Hegseth, whose loyalty may not protect his job as the Iran conflict continues.

items.subject: Michael Steele: A Total and Complete Schlonging
bullets: The MAGA coalition is fracturing as Fox News reels and Trump faces rejection from large swaths of the electorate, prompting Republicans who supported the ten‑year party hijack to seek redemption.
Steele praises recent DEI gains, noting a diverse slate of statewide winners and Texas’s dominance for GOP, while suggesting a national popular‑vote election is becoming more feasible.
The episode also speculates Marco Rubio’s likely departure from the administration and revisits Tim Miller’s 2012 ‘autopsy’ of the party’s direction.

items.subject: Trump’s ICE Backlash and Ohio’s Victory Dance
bullets: Adrian Carrasquillo argues that anger over Trump’s ICE policies shifted Latino voters toward Democrats, helping secure Ohio’s Democratic victory party.
Brendan Hartnett uses a ‘Cheesecake Factory’ metric to identify which House districts flipped Democratic, highlighting the narrow margins that decided the race.

Will Saletan and Joshua Tait examine how much Trump cost the GOP in the midterms and debate the party’s strategic path forward, with Bill Kristol and Mike Murphy discussing these issues on Sunday’s live show.

items.subject: This Week in Palestine: Two Babies Die in Gaza Tent Fire as UN Issues Dire Warning Ahead of Winter
bullets: Two infants died in a Gaza tent fire amid ongoing Israeli strikes that have killed nearly two dozen Palestinians, including children, this week.
The UN warned that the approaching winter will exacerbate humanitarian suffering in Gaza as the conflict continues.
In the West Bank, Israeli settlers seized Palestinian homes and the Israeli military compelled Palestinians to demolish their own houses.

items.subject: Dems Have Their Finger on the Impeachment Trigger
bullets: Rep. Robert Garcia, incoming House Oversight chair, is pushing Democrats to use the new majority to investigate Trump-era ICE and DHS abuses, citing voter anger and Latino backlash as key motivators.

Democratic leaders like Rep. Delia Ramirez and Sen. Ruben Gallego plan to build legal cases against ICE/DHS officials—especially Noem, Lewandowski, and former ICE director Todd Lyons—by documenting contract kickbacks, budget reallocation, and deadly inaction.

The agenda prioritizes accountability over retaliation, aiming to hold Trump administration officials criminally and politically responsible for deportation chaos, racial profiling, and the deaths of migrants such as Alex Pretti and Renée Good.

items.subject: Nate Silver: Trump’s Collapse May Be Irreversible
bullets: Tuesday night’s election results delivered the largest margin defeat for Donald Trump and MAGA to date, prompting questions about how much of the electorate remains contestable.
Nate Silver argues the scale of the loss signals a potentially irreversible collapse for Trump, with repercussions that could shape political dynamics well beyond the 2026 cycle.

items.subject: ‘MAGA Self-Immolated’: How EVERYTHING Fell Apart for Trump and Republicans This Year
bullets: Midterm elections produced a sweeping Democratic “blue tsunami,” with GOP losses in Senate, House, governors and traditionally red states like Texas and Kansas, far exceeding Trump‑aligned forecasts.

Trump’s attempts to influence the 2026 election and suppress Black voting were rebuffed by robust voting‑rights protections and a record‑high “Blacklash,” while massive spending by Elon Musk failed to rescue the party.

Prominent Republicans such as Ted Cruz and Ron DeSantis publicly distanced themselves from Trump as the GOP’s base fractured over unpopular policies, including the Iran war, economic woes, and anti‑immigrant rhetoric, leading to sharp declines among working‑class and Hispanic voters.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Can Democrats Finally Kill the Electoral College?
bullets: Pfeiffer argues that Democrats’ 2024 landslide could make any Republican in a district Trump won by less than 9 points unelectable, signaling a dramatic shift.

He explains the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which would allocate all state electoral votes to the national popular‑vote winner once states controlling 270 electoral votes join, offering a constitutional‑bypass route to end the Electoral College.

items.subject: Dems Aren’t Backing Off Their Own Redistricting Push
bullets: Democrats, fresh from sweeping midterm wins that gave them the House, Senate, governorships and most state legislatures, are already planning to resume mid‑decade redistricting efforts they paused last year.
Party officials told The Bulwark the redistricting drive is both an offensive tactic to capture additional House seats and a defensive hedge against GOP redistricting moves in Republican‑run states.
The top target states for the renewed Democratic redistricting push were not listed in the excerpt, but officials emphasized it as a “top agenda item” for the party.

items.subject: Talking to Martin Wolf About the Midterms
bullets: Krugman’s video features a conversation with FT columnist Martin Wolf analyzing the 2024 midterm elections and their implications for the Democratic agenda.

items.subject: Attrition Pocket
bullets: The Soviet‑built Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge in Kyiv, a vital Dnipro crossing for Western aid to Ukraine’s east front, was first hit by Russian drones and missiles in mid‑May, marking a shift to targeting key logistics after months of restraint.

Repeated strikes have forced partial or full closure of Kyiv’s major river bridges, threatening to sever supply lines that funnel shells, vehicles and fuel from the west to front‑line armies in the east.
Doomberg argues the delayed attacks signal a broader Russian strategy to split Ukraine and may presage a larger escalation they label a looming World War III scenario involving Iran.

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 94: Stephen Miller’s Promotion Shows Exactly What’s Ahead From Lame Duck Trump
bullets: Trump appointed Stephen Miller, the chief architect of his hard‑line immigration policies, as White House chief of staff on Nov. 6, signaling a continued authoritarian push despite his lame‑duck status.
Midterm results produced a historic Democratic wave: control of both chambers, the first Muslim senator (Abdul El‑Sayed), record women governors, and the first openly gay U.S. senator (Chris Pappas).

The DOJ moved again to vacate Steve Bannon’s 2022 contempt of Congress conviction, claiming doubts about trial fairness, while DHS claimed 300,000 non‑citizens on voter rolls despite evidence that non‑citizen voting is exceedingly rare.

items.subject: Abdul El-Sayed Talks to Zeteo About His Historic Victory
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed won Michigan’s Senate race by seven points, becoming the first Muslim U.S. senator despite record outside spending, Islamophobia and a split with Haley Stevens.
In a special interview, El‑Sayed says he’ll push Trump to sign a Medicare‑for‑All bill, hold the administration accountable for corruption, and hints at possible leadership changes in the Senate.
He also discusses J.D. Vance’s role in swearing him in, critiques the GOP’s midterm losses, and addresses racist backlash to his victory‑speech phrases “Inshallah” and “Alhamdulillah.”

items.subject: The All-Encompassing Terror of ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’
bullets: Godzilla Minus Zero hits IMAX this weekend with an overwhelming soundscape and graphic civilian casualties, earning an R‑rating for its vivid nuclear‑war imagery and anti‑heroic themes rooted in Japan’s wartime trauma.

The film continues the post‑Godzilla narrative two years later, focusing on emergency leader Mr. Noda, ex‑kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima, and their families as they confront the even louder, four‑headed Ghidorah.

The newsletter also notes the underwhelming effect of the vice president’s Texas swing on turnout and promotes a Bulwark+ flash sale plus a new interview with filmmaker Daniel Roher about his documentary ‘Navalny’ and the thriller ‘Tuner’.

items.subject: The Day After Deliverance
bullets: The Secret Podcast episode features Sarah and JVL reacting to recent political events, debating Democratic Congress actions, Trump‑related questions, and a satirical segment on Susan Collins, promoted with a 20% flash sale for Bulwark+ members.

items.subject: BREAKING: Trump Names Stephen Miller as Chief of Staff
bullets: Stephen Miller, Trump’s chief policy architect, was named White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles, amid a national blue wave that critics see as a rebuke of his hardline agenda.

Miller has engineered Trump’s most controversial policies, including mass deportations to third‑country prisons, the use of the Insurrection Act to justify deploying troops in urban areas, and targeted prosecutions of political opponents.

Sources claim Miller deliberately provoked unrest to create a pretext for military intervention, and he has openly advocated sending deportees to countries with poor human‑rights records to ensure compliance with U.S. demands.

items.subject: Trumpfall
bullets: The author claims Trump’s physical decline—obesity, fatigue, and health issues—has finally broken his once‑strong will to dominate after the election.
He argues that the post‑election accountability fight is now urgent, urging readers to join Bulwark+ with a 20% discount to support the effort.

bullets: Tim Miller, Sam Stein, and Will Sommer dissect the 2024 midterm, mocking JD Vance’s manosphere backlash, Tim Pool’s election breakdown, and MAGA defeats like Brandon Herrera’s loss, celebrating the GOP’s failures

Laura Loomer and Benny Johnson debate the results while Will Sommer introduces a prominent right‑wing streamer, highlighting his shocking living conditions, and notes Russell Brand’s rape conviction after a Trump‑era appearance

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Trump Got One Thing Right: We’re Not Tired of Winning
bullets: The 2024 midterms left the U.S. with 56 Democratic senators, ~260 Democratic House members, and Democratic governors in 13 of the 14 largest states, giving Democrats 60% of House seats and 70% of governorships.

Trump’s first post‑election act was an executive order designating the Oval Office a “national landmark,” a symbolic move that Kristol mocks as meaningless and uses to extend a celebratory weekend for Democrats.

Republicans’ heavy focus on trans‑panic ads in 2024 backfired; despite passing ballot measures restricting trans participation in sports, voters elected Democrats in key districts, showing that anti‑trans rhetoric was misread as a political advantage rather than a genuine policy shift.

items.subject: What many get wrong about Amish or Plain Anabaptist communities, measles, and health
bullets: Three unvaccinated measles deaths occurred this week in different states, the first such fatalities in over 30 years, highlighting reliance on herd immunity for infants too young to vaccinate.

Outbreaks are now emerging in Plain Anabaptist groups like the Amish and Mennonites, whose cultural practices and misconceptions about health complicate disease control, according to rural health researcher Tristan Sharratt.
Understanding these tight‑knit communities’ values and self‑protection strategies is essential for preventing a broader measles surge and improving overall health outreach.

items.subject: The Inconvenient Truth About Jewish Opinion on Zohran, Abdul, AIPAC, and Netanyahu
bullets: The newsletter argues that media outlets are applying a double or triple standard by linking criticism of Israel to anti‑Jewish sentiment, especially when left‑leaning figures like AOC gain traction.

It highlights a recent interview where Sara Haines asked Muslim senator‑elect Abdul El‑Sayed to address extremist views within Islam, noting the lack of comparable questioning of Christian or Jewish politicians.
The issue is framed alongside criticism of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s decisions and escalating concerns about Donald Trump’s approach to Iran.

items.subject: America’s Backlash Against Oligarchy
bullets: The 2022 midterms saw a broad voter backlash against Trump‑aligned policies, with the billionaire oligarch class—top 0.0001% now holding over seven times their 1980 wealth—spending heavily on Republicans yet losing key races, including Elon Musk’s >$200 million Texas effort that failed to keep Ken Paxton or a GOP governor.

Krugman argues that big money is self‑defeating: Republican messaging on the economy, health care, and the Iran war alienated voters, while the visible influence of oligarchic donors amplified perceptions of corruption, making wealth‑driven support a liability rather than an asset.

He identifies four limiting factors on oligarchic power—self‑defeating spending, corruption feedback, billionaire delusion, and party bubble‑ness—suggesting that without reforms to curb extreme wealth concentration, future elections will remain vulnerable to these same backlashes.

items.subject: Dems Put Up Saddam Numbers in Cheesecake Factory Districts
bullets: Obama’s joke likening Trump’s White House décor to “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory” sparked Republican outrage, framed as elitist snobbery against a symbol of middle‑class prosperity.

Despite the controversy, Democrats won 108 of the 175 congressional districts that contain a Cheesecake Factory, and under the 2026 map those restaurants sit in 171 districts, still favoring Democrats.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Why Democrats Won So Big
bullets: Democrats are on track for the largest House majority in decades and an unprecedented 56 Senate seats, far exceeding expectations for a ‘Blue Wave’.
Exit polls show 96% of voters said cost of living mattered, with 82% rating it very important, and they perceived Democrats as more focused on affordability than Republicans.

Pfeiffer warns that misreading this victory—like Republicans did after 1994 and 2010—could lead to strategic errors in candidate selection, electability narratives, and congressional priorities for the next two years.

items.subject: Trump’s Supreme Court Plans Just Hit a Massive Roadblock
bullets: Longwell and Weissmann argue that the recent judicial defeats of Trump’s election interference limit his ability to shape the Supreme Court, forcing a shift to congressional accountability measures.
They outline how Congress can use its new investigative powers and potential legislation to impose stronger guardrails on executive misconduct.
The episode promotes a 20% discount on Bulwark+ subscriptions, urging listeners to support continued coverage of these accountability efforts.

items.subject: Revenge of the (Democratic Budget) Nerds
bullets: Democratic leaders plan to restore Congress’s budgetary authority by targeting OMB Director Russell Vought, whom Rep. Brendan Boyle calls the “most dangerous man in America.”
Vought, a former Trump‑era official, is credited with enabling authoritarian budget moves and is described by Georgetown professor David A. Super as “evil” despite his competence.
The article outlines constitutional threats posed by Vought’s actions and urges the new Democratic majorities to use budget powers to reinstate separation of powers and punish him.

items.subject: MAGA Influencer Russell Brand Convicted of Rape
bullets: A UK jury convicted Russell Brand of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women for incidents between 2004 and 2009, and denied his bail request pending a significant prison term.

The conviction follows Brand’s rapid right‑wing shift since 2023, including appearances with Trump allies, a public conversion to Christianity, and participation in MAGA‑aligned events such as the 2024 RNC and 2025–2026 MAHA summits.

The article links Brand’s case to a broader pattern of sexual‑misconduct allegations among Trump‑associated figures, citing convictions and accusations against Donald Trump, Mike Tyson, Ted Nugent, George Nader, Pete Hegseth, Matt Gaetz, Elon Musk, and others.

items.subject: JD Vance Attacked His Faith. Now He’s Headed to the Senate. (w/ Adam Hamilton & Rob Flaherty)
bullets: Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton, upset by ICE policies, healthcare cuts and perceived Christian hypocrisy in D.C., defeated incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and is now senator‑elect.

Tim Miller’s show features Hamilton and former Kamala campaign staffer Rob Flaherty discussing the rise of midterm stars, Democratic messaging challenges, big GOP wins in GA, NC and PA, and the new Congress’s AI policy worries.
The episode also includes a interview with North Carolina’s Anderson Clayton and links to campaign ads and a ‘Nobody Knows Anything’ podcast from Flaherty.

items.subject: My Bar Crawl Through the MAGA Meltdown
bullets: Joe Perticone recounts being denied a reservation at Butterworth’s, a Capitol Hill bar popular with MAGA supporters, after security tightened for Election Night.
He planned to use the venue as a brief stop while covering chaotic watch parties, illustrating the clash of celebratory excess and political despair on election night.

items.subject: The Conspiracy to Push Donald Trump Aside
bullets: JD Vance launched his 2028 campaign by blaming Trump’s Iran policy, inflation, and close ties to Israel, urging Trump to surrender on Iran, cut ties with Israel, and drop tariffs to avoid Republican defeat.
Vance’s post suggests a coordinated effort with two other unnamed figures to push Trump out of the GOP race, though it’s unclear if Trump himself was involved in the strategy.

items.subject: The World’s Most Powerful Government Is Targeting This Man for Pro-Palestine Speech
bullets: Georgetown scholar Badar Khan Suri, an Indian legal resident, was detained for two months by ICE and targeted for deportation after criticizing Israel’s Gaza assault, sparking a federal judge’s release order.
The U.S. government’s renewed deportation effort could set a precedent for using immigration enforcement to punish pro‑Palestine speech, raising concerns about free‑speech limits.
Suri’s case highlights the personal toll of such crackdowns, as he endured multiple facility transfers, family separation, and costly legal battles while advocating for democracy and Gaza’s plight.

items.subject: The Right’s Election Meltdown Is Just Getting Started
bullets: Conservative influencers like Benny Johnson rode a brief high from a 1,020‑vote GOP win in Guam, then pivoted to despair as Democrats secured a massive House sweep and at least 54 Senate seats.

Midterm losses sparked infighting: Dave Smith clashed with Jack Posobiec on Piers Morgan, Matt Walsh advocated a nuclear‑armed Iran to block a ‘Communist’ win, and Liz Wheeler blamed the Justice Department’s inaction for GOP defeat.

Republican leaders, including JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., and Ron DeSantis, blamed the Iran war and demographic shifts, while far‑right figures like Laura Loomer warned of an ‘Islamic takeover’ and questioned their faith.

items.newsletter: Here Be Dragons from Barbara F. Walter
items.subject: Eight Things We Learned From the Midterms
bullets: Nearly 124.3 million Americans voted in the midterms—about 12 million more than 2022—making it the second‑highest turnout since 1914, with 70 % of voters under 30 favoring Democrats; 58 % of Latino men and 69 % of Latino women voted Democratic, reversing Trump’s 2024 gains; white women shifted from a 10‑point Trump advantage to a narrow Democratic edge, while white evangelical Christians remained 80 % Republican; Democrats captured governorships and flipped legislative chambers in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Texas, giving them control over state election rules through 2028; no significant election misconduct was reported, and Trump accepted the results, signaling a potential end to post‑election contestation.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Here’s What Happens When Trump’s Star Implodes
bullets: The midterm election saw a dramatic blue wave, highlighted by Democrat Zach Dembo’s 9‑point win in Kentucky’s 6th District, signaling a massive shift toward Democrats nationwide.

Vice President J.D. Vance publicly blamed the GOP’s loss on the Iran war and called for a pivot to cost‑of‑living issues, Israel policy changes, and ending the war—an unprecedented critique from a Trump ally.

Trump’s own response was detached, focusing on personal projects like a new East Wing ballroom while the GOP, including figures like DeSantis and Carlson, openly questioned his leadership and the future of the party.

items.subject: 🫣 Republicans Groan: Trump and Stephen Miller ‘Screwed’ Us, and Killed Our 2026 Dreams!
bullets: Republican elites blame President Trump and his adviser Stephen Miller for the GOP’s 2026 midterm losses, citing Trump’s illegal Iran war, rising costs, and mass deportations that eroded Hispanic support.

The blame focuses on Trump’s policy failures—particularly the 2024 immigration crackdown and the “War Secretary” Pete Hegseth’s Iran campaign—while Miller’s domestic agenda is singled out for causing voter backlash.
The narrative frames the GOP’s defeat as a direct result of Trump’s actions, with donors and lawmakers reluctant to name him publicly due to fear of backlash and career damage.

items.subject: Chase Your Phantoms
bullets: James Horton shifted to a 25‑hour circadian rhythm in late 2025, eliminating morning grogginess and seasonal depression, but discovered Wellbutrin XL causes cloud‑brain when not depressed, leading to a summer of mental fog.

He completed two of four 8,000‑word academic journal articles, delaying Substack output; his pattern of “purpose creep” has inflated his posts to over 3,000 words, prompting a new strategy to finish one long piece per month while experimenting with shorter formats.

items.subject: What Democrats Can Do
bullets: Democrats should use their new committee control to launch subpoenas exposing Trump’s corruption while passing popular, progressive legislation—like ACA subsidy restoration, Medicare expansions, and stronger Ukraine aid—knowing Trump will veto and forcing Republican votes on overrides.

By forcing Trump’s vetoes on well‑crafted bills, Democrats can highlight Republican complicity, potentially win some GOP overrides on issues such as sanctions on Russia, and build a policy platform for the 2028 elections.
Krugman notes the market’s reaction: oil prices fell and the Dow rose 1,500 points after the midterms, reflecting reduced war risk despite Trump’s continued veto power.

items.subject: Trump’s Crushing Defeat Just Changed How the World Sees America
bullets: Former CIA officer Marc Polymeropoulos and journalist Michael Weiss argue that Trump’s midterm losses have prompted allies to celebrate, seeing a shift away from his destabilizing foreign policy.
They warn the results empower Ukraine against Russia, constrain Iran’s aggression, and expose Netanyahu’s gamble on MAGA as costly for Israel.
The hosts predict intense congressional investigations of Trump’s inner circle and forecast that JD Vance and Elon Musk will suffer major political setbacks from the election outcome.

items.subject: Will Sommer & Sam Stein: MAGA is Losing Their Effing Minds
bullets: Donald Trump ignored the midterm defeat, instead touring a White House ballroom construction site to admire chandeliers, kitchen layouts and a steel beam, prioritizing a vanity project over political fallout.

Republican leaders such as Laura Loomer, Marjorie Taylor Greene, Mark Levin, and Nancy Mace engaged in a heated blame game, trading insults and pointing fingers at each other for the losses, while Trump remained absent from the scene.

items.subject: Will the Democratic Leadership Dare to Be Bold?
bullets: The 2026 midterms saw Democrats win Senate seats in Kansas, Maine, Ohio, Iowa, North Carolina (20‑point margin), South Carolina (4‑point margin) and Texas (James Talarico beat Ken Paxton by 12 points), giving the party 54‑56 Senate seats in 2027 and likely 250+ House seats.

The massive Democratic majorities mean no single caucus—whether the left‑leaning “Squad” or centrist figures like Senator John Fetterman—can control the agenda, but they also face high expectations to act decisively against the Trump administration amid a party split on ideology and tactics.

items.subject: Sh*t Just Got a Lot Easier for the Democratic Party Project
bullets: Trump’s 2016 win shattered Democratic confidence, leading to a defensive posture that treated large swaths of the country as unwinnable; recent 2024 results challenge that narrative.

In 2024, Democrats won key Senate races—Cooper (NC), Talarico (TX), Andrews (SC), Hamilton (KS), Brown (OH), Turek (IA)—and flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, and Nevada, plus major state‑legislature gains.

items.subject: Fox Finds Itself In a ‘Hell of a Pickle’ as America Turns on Trump
bullets: Fox News struggled to blame Trump for the 2024 blue wave, yet avoided attacking him, revealing a deep identity crisis as the network tries to pivot while still tied to his brand.

The network’s election‑night coverage devolved into a prolonged struggle session, with hosts scrambling for excuses to explain the GOP’s blowout, highlighting their inability to distance themselves from Trump’s influence.

items.subject: ‘Latino Fury’: How Anti-ICE Fervor Helped Democrats Take Back Congress
bullets: Latino voters swung decisively toward Democrats in 2024, driven by anti‑ICE sentiment and economic concerns, with Latino turnout in Texas’s Rio Grande Valley surpassing 2024 levels and a 70‑point swing for Democrat James Talarico in 97‑percent Latino Starr County.

Talarico’s campaign spent over $16 million on TV ads, including $5 million on primary TV and $10 million in the fall, using stark language about ICE as a “secret police force” and highlighting the kidnapping of children to galvanize Latino voters.

Democratic consultants ran targeted Spanish‑language ads across red states—Kansas, Nebraska, Texas—emphasizing ICE abuses and Trump’s immigration policies, successfully unseating Republican incumbents like Monica De La Cruz in Texas’s 15th Congressional District.

items.subject: State of the Themes
bullets: Citrindex’s total return has outperformed the S&P 500 by over 2.5x since its May 31 2023 launch, but rising valuations have pushed thematic ideas from cheap winners to speculative, unprofitable 2030‑TAM bets.

The newsletter warns that AI capex is peaking: hyperscalers face a $1 trillion annual spend gap, with revenue growth lagging and datacenter bottlenecks and financing strain threatening further expansion.

Citrini is overhauling the Citrindex, shifting from continuation trades to reversals, pairs and fresh ideas, while adding new sectors like Boomer Software, Booze & Bubbles, Financials and Entertainment.

items.subject: 9 Impressive Midterm Wins You May Have Missed From the Blue Tsunami
bullets: Democrats and progressives scored a sweeping midterm victory, dubbed a “blue tsunami,” overturning Trump‑aligned anti‑DEI, anti‑immigrant, and misogynistic rhetoric across multiple states.

Key upsets included Abdul El‑Sayed’s win in Michigan, James Talarico’s victory in Texas, and Keisha Lance Bottoms’ success in Georgia, alongside numerous lesser‑known races that underscored the shift.
The newsletter highlights nine additional wins—such as historic victories for Black women in Georgia—demonstrating the breadth of Democratic gains and the failure of Trump’s policy agenda.

items.subject: It Happened!
bullets: The 2024 election delivered a historic rejection of Trump and MAGA, with Democrats winning key races and former Trump voters shifting away from the GOP, according to Tim Miller, Sarah Longwell, and JVL.

JD Vance is attempting a notable break from Trump, distancing himself from the former president’s Iran war stance, while analysts discuss potential Republican civil war and implications for the Supreme Court and 2028 balance of power.
The Bulwark is offering a flash 20% discount on Bulwark+ subscriptions through Friday, inviting new members to join as the political landscape shifts.

items.subject: This is our moment. Let’s seize it.
bullets: The 2024 midterms delivered a decisive rebuke of Donald Trump, with a clear blue wave that the author credits to organized voter mobilization and coalition building.
The Bulwark plans to capitalize on this momentum by intensifying investigative reporting, expanding analysis, and encouraging community engagement to sustain democratic gains over the next 24 months.
A 20% flash sale on Bulwark+ is offered to attract new members, framing the subscription as a way to join the ongoing fight against authoritarianism.

items.subject: Thank you, New Hampshire
bullets: Chris Pappas won New Hampshire’s U.S. Senate seat, defeating a $67 million attack campaign from Trump, Musk and corporate interests, and vows to bring independent leadership to Washington.

He pledges to tackle key issues—housing, health care, child care, Social Security, climate protection, reproductive freedom, corruption, and administration accountability—while urging New Hampshire voters to stay persistent and united.

items.subject: I’m ready.
bullets: The author recounts a Texas rally where 1.6 million COVID‑19 deaths, measles outbreaks, job losses, Medicaid cuts, and rising medical debt illustrate a 7‑year public health collapse.

He highlights a record wave of STEM professionals—pediatrician, public health physician, microbiologist, nuclear engineer, ER nurse, environmental engineer, mathematician—winning state and federal seats, signaling a shift toward science‑driven policy.

He calls for a decade‑long, inclusive overhaul of the health system, arguing that repair alone is insufficient and that community expertise, lived experience, and innovative strategy are essential to rebuild a responsive, accountable ecosystem.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Too Big to Rig
bullets: The 2026 election produced a Democratic landslide—up to a 14‑point popular‑vote margin, roughly 45 House seats and 7‑9 Senate seats gained, plus majorities in most governorships—making the wave “too big to rig.”
Andrew Egger argues Trump’s post‑2020 election‑fraud scheme is now dead, as the Democratic sweep eliminates the institutional support he would need to attempt another steal in 2028.
Bill Kristol warns Republicans face a bind: tied to a lame‑duck Trump with no alternative power bases, while internal factional fights over issues like the Iran war will intensify.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: A Republican Wipeout for the Ages
bullets: Democrats won the 2026 midterms with the largest popular‑vote margin since 1974, flipping the House, Senate, and key states like Georgia, Texas, Arizona, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Michigan, and electing a Black woman governor in Georgia and a Latina governor in Texas.

The Republican coalition collapsed: Trump’s approval fell to 38%, 70% of Trump‑voters chose Democrats, white voters without college degrees swung 10 points toward Democrats, and rural voters shifted from a 30‑point Trump lead in 2024 to an 18‑point lead in 2026, enabling Democratic gains in South Carolina, Texas, Kansas, and Iowa.

Democratic candidates drove the turnaround by energizing bases and capturing 6% of Republican votes nationwide, with standout cross‑party wins such as Adam Hamilton (12% of Republicans in Kansas), Talarico (11% in Kansas), and Annie Andrews (11% in South Carolina), while Trump’s strategic missteps—endorsing Ken Paxton, pushing out Thom Tillis, selecting JD Vance as VP, and backing under‑qualified candidates—cost the GOP millions and opened winnable seats to Democrats.

items.subject: Republicans’ 2026 ‘Bloodbath’ Was Way Worse Than Trumpland Expected
bullets: The 2026 midterms delivered a “bloodbath” for Republicans, with Democratic gains in Michigan, Maine, Ohio and other key states, sending new Democratic senators to Capitol Hill and signaling a major blow to Trump’s agenda.

Republican insiders, including senior Trump administration officials, were shocked by the scale of losses, especially the unexpected Democratic swing in Texas, which exceeded their worst‑case scenarios and marked a catastrophic repudiation of Trump’s war, economic, and corruption policies.
The election results are portrayed as a decisive defeat for Trump’s fascist presidency, implying significant political and strategic setbacks for the GOP over the next two years.

items.subject: It Wasn’t (Just) the Economy, Stupid
bullets: The 2024 election saw Democrats win the popular vote by 13‑14 points, driven by Hispanic voters rejecting Trump’s promises and Black voters turning out against a racist party, while Trump’s economic claims failed to hold up.

Trump’s administration’s aggressive immigration policies, corruption, and perceived authoritarianism alienated diverse American groups, leading to a mass rejection of fascist rhetoric and a reaffirmation of democratic values.

items.subject: Recycle Bin
bullets: US natural gas output is projected to exceed the entire EU’s total in 2026 and repeat in 2027, driving spot prices down to $1‑2 per MMBtu ($6‑12 per barrel).

EQT is acquiring Range Resources in a $13 billion all‑stock deal, creating the nation’s largest gas producer as firms scramble to lock in supply for upcoming LNG export terminals and gas‑fired data‑center power plants.

A severe shortage of gas‑turbine generators—back‑ordered until 2030‑2032—threatens to bottleneck the conversion of abundant shale gas into electricity, prompting speculation about repurposing used aircraft engines.

items.subject: Blue Tsunami: Watch Zeteo’s Coverage with Mehdi, Prem, Mallory McMorrow, Jamaal Bowman, Rep. Greg Casar, and More!
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed won Michigan’s Senate race, becoming the first Muslim U.S. senator, as Democrats seized control of both the House and Senate in a “blue tsunami.”

The Zeteo live stream featured guests like Rep. Greg Casar, UAW president Shawn Fain, and others, with Mallory McMorrow urging a grassroots overhaul of the Democratic Party and Jamal Bowman calling Haley Stevens the “ultimate villain” of the American reckoning.
In Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy suffered a decisive loss to Democrat Amy Acton in the governor’s race, while Mehdi and Prem criticized Elon Musk’s failed attempt to keep Texas red.

items.subject: BREAKING: Dems Take Full Control of Congress in Trump-GOP Disaster
bullets: Democrats secured a sweeping victory, gaining a decisive House majority and flipping seven Senate seats, including historic wins in Kansas (first Democratic senator since 1932) and Texas (first Senate seat for Democrats since 1988).
Trump acknowledged the results, claiming he’ll accept them and asserting a veto power, while Democrats now can launch formal investigations and block his agenda with control of both chambers.

Key races: Adam Hamilton (D) beat GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas; Sherrod Brown (D) reclaimed Ohio seat; Annie Andrews (D) unseated appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, a loss linked to Graham’s support for a U.S.-Israeli war in Iran.

items.subject: Emergency Triad: MAGA Drowns Under a Blue Wave
bullets: Democrats are on track to control 55‑56 Senate seats and a solid House majority, giving the new speaker leeway and opening the door to possible impeachment votes against Trump‑aligned officials.

The author urges aggressive legal preparation for anyone tied to Trump’s enterprises and stresses that Democrats must keep pressuring Republicans with votes on issues like the Iran war, Epstein files, and impeachment to prevent a post‑Trump GOP resurgence.

Key races highlighted include Gina Hinojosa’s upset in Texas, Annie Andrews’ win, and the near‑defeat of Susan Collins, signaling a generational realignment that still requires a decade of work to fully dismantle Trumpism.

items.subject: *STREAM NOW* Mehdi and Prem Are Live From Michigan!
bullets: The Zeteo live stream from Detroit covers the 2026 midterm results, focusing on tight Senate races in Michigan and Texas, with on‑the‑ground interviews including Michigan candidate Abdul El‑Sayed, Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud, and former Rep. Andy Levin.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: The Election Night Group Chat is live
bullets: Dan Pfeiffer invites subscribers to a live Election Night Group Chat for real‑time results, Q&A, and his analysis, with an hour‑by‑hour guide to key races.
He’ll be present all night except when on TV or recording Pod Save America, and non‑subscribers are urged to upgrade to join.

items.subject: Tonight: We’re going live starting at 7 p.m. EST
bullets: The Bulwark will stream live Election Night coverage with Tim Miller, Sarah Longwell, JVL and guests across Substack, YouTube, Facebook, and Twitch starting at 7 p.m. EST.

items.subject: Would Trump Actually Nuke Iran? Probably Not
bullets: Tucker Carlson’s tweet claiming the Trump administration is days from a nuclear strike on Iran is likely a fabricated “leak” meant to generate hype, not evidence of actual plans.
The author argues Trump is unlikely to use nuclear weapons, noting the administration’s pattern of releasing hypothetical war or peace scenarios to pressure Tehran and calm markets.
The live election coverage tonight will feature hosts Mehdi, Prem, Swin, and Andrew reporting from various locations, discussing these claims among other topics.

items.subject: AOC Quietly Lays the Groundwork
bullets: AOC’s late‑stage Virginia tour, boosting moderate Democrat Rep. Eugene Vindman, signals she’s building goodwill in the state that will vote sixth in the 2028 Democratic primary, positioning her for a possible presidential run.

The event highlighted a rare alliance between AOC and centrist Governor Abigail Spanberger, whose 2025 gubernatorial campaign AOC is now fundraising for, underscoring a broader Democratic strategy to unite progressives and moderates in purple districts.

AOC’s campaign memo details her extensive multi‑state stump‑tour, fundraising strength, and intent to remain a key endorsement engine, while Democrats view Virginia’s shifting, educated electorate as a crucial early‑primary battleground for 2028.

items.subject: Navigating the Chaos
bullets: Paul Krugman has released an ebook compiling his Substack posts, organized by theme and presented as a chronicle of recent disturbing events.
The collection includes additional material that outlines each theme, providing context for the original posts.
The ebook is available on Amazon via the provided Substack redirect link.

items.subject: Brendan Boyle Has a Warning for Trump’s Project 2025 Mastermind
bullets: Rep. Brendan Boyle outlines Democrats’ strategy to reverse Trump’s healthcare cuts, tariffs, and address economic fallout from the Iran war if they regain the House.
Catherine Rampell and Sam Stein preview Election Day, noting Trump’s focus on the economy and how rising costs and voter frustration could influence turnout and results.

items.subject: 💬 New thread from The Bulwark
bullets: The Bulwark launches a live Election Day coverage at 7 p.m. ET featuring hosts Tim, Sarah, and JVL, with updates from Ohio, Michigan, Texas, Georgia, and Washington, D.C.
Viewers can join the live stream on Substack, YouTube, Facebook, and Twitch, and participate in the chat to predict House and Senate outcomes and potential surprise races.

items.subject: *STREAM TONIGHT* Mehdi and Prem Are Going Live From Michigan
bullets: Zeteo will livestream the 2026 midterm night starting at 9pm ET, covering Detroit’s Senate race between Abdul El‑Sayed and Mike Rogers with on‑ground commentary from Mehdi and Prem.
Swin Suebsaeng will join the stream to cover Ohio’s gubernatorial race featuring Vivek Ramasawmy, while Andrew Perez will report on the outcome of Sen. Susan Collins’ race in Maine.
The livestream is free for subscribers; additional support can be given via paid subscription or donation links provided in the email.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: The Alex Pretti Election
bullets: Andrew Egger argues Trump’s 2025 downfall began with Minneapolis, where federal ICE occupation, violent clashes, and the deaths of Renée Good and Alex Pretti sparked nationwide backlash that forced the White House to abandon blue‑city enforcement and weakened Trump’s unilateral state power.

Egger links the Minneapolis resistance to a broader pattern of Trump’s state violence against Democratic protesters, noting that similar DHS killings (Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero) and lack of accountability further eroded public support.

The article suggests that if voters respond to this resistance, Democrats may regain control, but even if not, Minneapolis offers a model of grassroots opposition that could limit future executive overreach.

items.subject: Election stress and your heart, early flu, another CDC leader leaves, and a mom’s hard question about vaccine inju…
bullets: Election‑day stress is linked to higher heart‑rhythm abnormalities: a 2016 study of 2,436 North Carolina patients found a 77% increase during the election window, and a 2020 Kaiser Permanente analysis of 6.4 million Californians showed a 17% rise in cardiovascular hospitalizations and a 42% rise in heart‑attack admissions in the five days after the election.

Early U.S. flu season is normal but accelerating: every region now has >3% test positivity, with 60‑80 flu‑related deaths per week and a projected peak of ~1,800; CDC forecasts the season to resemble last winter, and Canadian data show all 116 samples match the current vaccine strains, suggesting good vaccine‑virus match.

items.subject: What About Arab and Muslim Safety?
bullets: Prem reports from Dearborn that Michigan Rep. Alabas Farhat, a 26‑year‑old Muslim lawmaker, highlighted how state policies suppress free speech and fund Israel under the guise of ‘Jewish safety’ while neglecting Arab and Muslim protection.

The newsletter claims corporate media ignores the campaign’s focus on anti‑Muslim rhetoric, noting that Donald Trump’s administration and Republican control have intensified Islamophobia, including attempts to ban, criminalize, deport, and bomb Muslim‑looking individuals.

It also notes recent political developments: the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s bid to discard 20,000 California ballots, Trump is poised to pre‑emptively pardon Elon Musk, and a pardoned Jan. 6 defendant faces charges for threatening judges.

items.subject: Today is Election Day. Let’s finish this strong.
bullets: Roy Cooper urges North Carolinians to vote today, emphasizing that the election can reverse policies he calls harmful—war, costly healthcare, rising grocery and gas prices—by electing a pro‑working‑family senator.
He thanks volunteers for 15 months of canvassing, phone calls, and donations, framing the campaign as a hopeful movement to flip North Carolina blue.
Cooper provides a polling‑place link and reminds voters that lines open at 7:30 PM will be honored, urging people to bring a friend and encourage neighbors to vote.

items.subject: It’s Election Day
bullets: Chris Pappas, whose family’s Manchester restaurant has operated 109 years and churns over 35,000 gallons of ice cream annually, is urging New Hampshire voters to turn out for his Senate race against John Sununu.
He highlights his bipartisan record in Congress, his LGBTQ+ identity, and his claim that the Trump‑aligned GOP agenda threatens reproductive rights and raises costs for families.
Pappas frames the election as a fight for a fair economy, urging every Granite State voter to vote via IWillVote.com/NH to prevent a return to “extreme rhetoric” and billionaire‑focused policies.

items.subject: Moment of Truth
bullets: Polls, expert analyses and prediction markets indicate Democrats have a solid lead in the House and about an 80% probability of winning the Senate.
Krugman expresses personal anxiety about the election, noting the stakes feel like the nation’s soul is on the line.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: An Hour-by-Hour Guide to Staying Sane on Election Night.
