bullets: Midterm races span a larger map than presidential ones, with many contests in traditionally Republican states like Kansas, Mississippi and Alaska, making the Democratic advantage harder to gauge.
Polls favor Democrats but key Senate races in GOP states are expected to be tighter than polls suggest because remaining undecided voters are largely Trump supporters.

Pfeiffer’s hour‑by‑hour guide highlights early toss‑up contests in Indiana’s 5th and Kentucky’s 6th districts, and a pivotal Georgia governor race where a Keisha Lance Bottoms win could affect future House maps and an Ossoff presidential bid.

items.subject: Mike Madrid Predicts a Political Earthquake in Texas
bullets: Mike Madrid, a 35‑year veteran on Latino voters, says turnout data shows unprecedented engagement that could destabilize Trump’s 2024 coalition and enable a Democratic upset in Texas.
Conway argues that Trump’s gerrymandering plan may unintentionally give Democrats additional House seats, while a Republican sweep looks increasingly unlikely.
The discussion also covers Haley Stevens’ unexpected endorsement of Mike Rogers in Michigan, highlighting shifting intra‑party dynamics.

items.subject: Two sentences
bullets: Chris Pappas asks readers to donate $15 immediately to help meet a $300,000 fundraising target aimed at turning out voters and keeping New Hampshire blue in tomorrow's Senate race.

items.subject: Bill Kristol Thinks Trump's GOP Is About to Get Wiped Out (Plus: JVL!)
bullets: Bill Kristol warns that the GOP’s alignment with Trump is on the brink of collapse as midterm dynamics shift, especially after the Iran war debate and Democratic poll leads.
A Democratic senator described the administration’s Iran war plan as ‘insane,’ warning it could trigger a devastating escalation, adding pressure on the president’s Middle East strategy.

items.subject: Watch Mehdi Call Out ‘Charlatan’ Haley Stevens on ‘Piers Morgan Uncensored’
bullets: Mehdi Hasan told Piers Morgan that Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens fabricated an antisemitic ad controversy as a pretext to withdraw support from Democrat Abdul El‑Sayed and back Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers.

Hasan argued the real scandal is the White House’s “old school white supremacist” rhetoric, citing Islamophobic attacks on El‑Sayed, a recent antisemitic slur by the president, and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins’ racist Halloween post.

items.subject: MAGA Preps for the World to End—Literally
bullets: Glenn Beck and other pro‑Trump media personalities are warning their audiences to “prepare for impact,” claiming an unnamed apocalyptic event—war, cyberattack or otherwise—is imminent despite no evidence.

The apocalyptic narrative has been amplified by figures like former FBI deputy director Dan Bongino and even prompted a Republican congressman to publicly deny any imminent “shit hitting the fan,” while right‑wing prep guides flood online forums.

If current polls hold, the GOP could suffer a crushing midterm loss within 24 hours, a defeat that many on the right fear could signal a broader civilizational collapse they link to the alleged hidden global threat.

items.subject: I can win again, but only with your help.
bullets: Senator Jon Ossoff urges supporters to donate, claiming his Georgia Senate seat is the only Democratic one up for reelection in a state Trump won and is vital for Senate control.
He argues the current administration is abusing power, driving war and inflation, and that winning his race is essential to protect checks and balances and free elections in 2028.
The email includes direct ActBlue donation links, asking for contributions of any size, especially $10, to fund voter outreach and his campaign.

items.subject: Final Senate Polls Are So Good, Sarah Can Barely Believe Them
bullets: Final Senate polls show Democrats ahead, but Sarah doubts their accuracy amid low early voting and fears a Republican turnout collapse.
Rising gas prices could become Trump’s biggest electoral liability, according to the newsletter.
The episode teases JD Vance’s harsh New York Times coverage, Peggy Noonan’s MAGA redemption narrative, and Haley Stevens' surprising weekend events.

items.subject: How Elon Musk Bought the Midterms. We Did the Math
bullets: Elon Musk spent $474 million on 2026 Republican candidates, the largest single‑donor contribution in U.S. history, to help Donald Trump maintain control of Congress and undermine democratic norms.
The $474 million equals about 0.05% of Musk’s net worth and is roughly the same amount a median American could spend on a video game and a coffee tumbler.

items.subject: A Close-Up View of the Wildest 24 Hours of the El-Sayed Campaign
bullets: Abdul El‑Sayed’s Sunday press conference at a black church was derailed by Rep. Haley Stevens’ surprise endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers, sparking a media frenzy and a rift within the Michigan Democratic Party.

El‑Sayed’s campaign raised $2.4 million in the hours after Stevens’ endorsement and an 11‑point lead in a New York Times/Siena poll, but his campaign is battling anti‑Arab and anti‑Muslim ads that tap into bigotry.

Stevens’ public endorsement of Rogers, her subsequent CNN interview, and the withdrawal of a planned joint appearance with El‑Sayed highlight deep divisions over El‑Sayed’s Israel‑related rhetoric and the broader Democratic strategy for Michigan’s Senate race.

items.subject: The local reporter who took the government to court twice
bullets: Laura Belin, a Des Moines reporter, sued the Iowa governor’s office over pandemic open‑records violations and the House chief clerk after being denied press credentials, with legal fees covered by the Institute for Free Speech and reader donations.

She produces niche, in‑depth Iowa political coverage—early voting data, election‑worker prosecutions, and exclusive scoops like Senator Grassley’s hot‑mic slip—often after being barred from campaign events such as GOP gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn’s rallies.

Through the Iowa Writers Collaborative she runs a free Substack, now earning a salary, and highlights how a network of ~70 local newsletters is reviving regional journalism as legacy papers shut down.

items.subject: I Believe in the Kaiju Tsunami
bullets: The author says the probabilistic model for Senate seats has shifted from a modal outcome of 52 Democratic seats a month ago to about 53‑54 seats today, with the wave gaining momentum.
He argues the most likely result is now 53 or 54 Democratic senators, but hints he will place his money on a different outcome altogether.

items.subject: Blue Texas Is a Mirage—Until It Isn’t
bullets: At a Trump‑backed rally in Weatherford, over 1,000 mostly Republican voters heard speakers warn of “trans ideology” and attack Democrat James Talarico, illustrating GOP’s fear‑based strategy in Texas.

Exit polls showed Trump captured about 55% of the Hispanic vote in 2024, but recent data indicate a sharp swing back to Democrats, with Latino voters now favoring Talarico over Paxton by double digits and half of 760,000 new early voters being Hispanic.

Republican officials, including state comptroller Don Huffines, acknowledged a 600,000‑vote deficit to Democrats after early voting, prompting GOP leaders to shift focus northward as southern Texas turnout surges.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: It Won’t Be a Blue Tsunami. It’ll Be an Orange Crush.
bullets: Kristol argues the 2026 midterms will deliver a decisive Democratic wave, with NYT/Siena polls showing Democrats ahead in six of seven battleground Senate states—including Texas and Kansas—and likely flipping both chambers and key governorships, effectively repudiating Trumpism.
He urges immediate voter turnout, noting over 50 million early votes already cast and stressing that tens of millions more must vote to cement this shift.

Mark Hertling highlights Trump’s recent anti‑Norway rant, noting Norway’s modest 5.6 million population, strong NATO contributions (9,200 troops in Afghanistan, ten killed), and cultural values of humility and community that clash with Trump’s worldview.

items.subject: Haley Stevens Called ‘MAGA Mike’ Wrong for Michigan – Then Stabbed El-Sayed and Dems in the Back
bullets: Rep. Haley Stevens announced she will vote for Trump‑aligned Rep. Mike Rogers, denouncing Abdul El‑Sayed and sparking outrage from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who called it a “despicable betrayal.”
The move comes days before the midterms amid ongoing Trump‑backed election lawsuits, with judges in Alaska and California temporarily blocking some of the administration’s challenges.
Zeteo will broadcast live election‑night coverage from El‑Sayed’s Detroit HQ, with reporters in Ohio and Maine, urging free subscribers to upgrade for full access.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: New NYT Polls Point to a Blue Tsunami
bullets: The new NYT/Siena polls show Democrats leading in all seven Senate battlegrounds, including double‑digit leads in Michigan, 7‑point lead in Texas, and 5‑point lead in Kansas, suggesting a potential blue wave.
Pfeiffer argues the poll margins may be unusually favorable to Democrats and cautions they could be too good to be true, noting even top pollsters can err.
He promotes a paid subscription for an hour‑by‑hour Election Night guide, live chat, and post‑election analysis, with further coverage planned through 2028.

items.subject: Oligarchy is on the Ballot
bullets: Only 20 ultra‑rich donors—about one ten‑millionth of the U.S. adult population—have contributed roughly $2 billion, or 15% of total midterm spending, overwhelmingly to Republican candidates.

The author argues that this oligarchic funding, enabled by Citizens United and a century‑long surge in wealth concentration, threatens a Democratic Congress that might investigate Trump‑linked corruption.
Polls show Republicans likely to lose the House and possibly the Senate, making the midterms a test of whether the wealthy can still ‘own’ the government.

items.subject: Zeteo’s Indispensable Midterms Guide, Breaking Down the Key 2026 Races
bullets: Trump’s authoritarian actions and economic policies have made the 2026 midterms a pivotal chance for Democrats to impose checks, with Republicans risking backlash for supporting his war stance and ICE tactics.

The Senate currently stands at a 53‑47 Republican majority; Democrats need to net four seats—potentially five if Senator John Fetterman departs—to flip control, overturning the tie‑breaker role of Vice President JD Vance.

items.subject: Live video with The Bulwark now: Pre-Election Livestream
bullets: The Bulwark’s paid‑subscriber livestream titled “Pre‑Election Livestream” is now live, offering a live video discussion for subscribers.

items.subject: Inside the Wargaming to Foil Trump’s Election Meddling
bullets: Around 250 ACLU lawyers and experts convened in Philadelphia to wargame 25 Trump‑related election‑interference scenarios, drafting mock press releases and state‑specific legal and organizing responses.
The meeting coincided with the Supreme Court’s decision to gut Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, prompting rapid Republican redistricting that threatened Black voting power in the South.
ACLU officials warned that midterms will face unprecedented challenges from election deniers in key state administration roles, and they claim to be prepared on all fronts.

items.subject: Our last chance
bullets: The newsletter urges New Hampshire voters to turn out on Nov 3, noting over 90% vote that day and that the state’s Senate race could flip the U.S. Senate.
Pappas launches a “Last Chance Fund” aiming to raise $300,000 by Nov 3, asking for $15 donations to power voter outreach and keep New Hampshire blue.
He warns GOP candidate John Sununu leads in polls after $67 million of Republican spending, stressing the need for immediate grassroots contributions.

items.subject: Zeteo Is Going LIVE for the Midterms, and We Need Your Support To Do It!
bullets: Zeteo will broadcast live election night coverage on Substack and YouTube from 9 pm ET, with Mehdi and Prem at Abdul El‑Sayed HQ in Detroit, Swin Suebsaeng reporting from Ohio races, and Andrew Perez covering Susan Collins in Maine.

The outlet, fully subscriber‑funded, urges free subscribers to upgrade to paid this week to unlock in‑depth reporting and documentaries, and invites donations to sustain independent, unfiltered coverage.

items.subject: Join Us Tonight To Kick Off Election Week
bullets: The Bulwark is hosting a members‑only midterms livestream tonight at 8:30 p.m. EST, featuring Tim, Sam, Andrew and reporters Joe Perticone, Lauren Egan, and Jonathan Cohn to dissect key races and surprises.
They’re urging non‑subscribers to join now for access to the livestream, exclusive content, and to participate in a Q&A without scripted talking points.

items.subject: 48 Hours
bullets: More than 2.8 million North Carolinians have already voted early, but the race remains tight and could be decided by a few thousand or fewer votes.
Volunteers are urged to knock doors, make calls, and offer rides in the final 48 hours before Election Day to get remaining voters to the polls.
Supporters can sign up to volunteer or donate via the provided links, as every shift and contribution could tip the margin.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Quick Thoughts on the Impact of Haley Stevens’ Stunning Betrayal
bullets: Haley Stevens, after narrowly losing her primary, reversed her endorsement and backed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, despite previously supporting Democrat Abdul El‑Sayed to block Trump.
The author notes El‑Sayed leads Nate Silver’s poll average by 4.1 points, but warns the GOP’s extreme anti‑Muslim campaign could jeopardize the Democratic advantage.
Stevens’ flip is portrayed as a potentially decisive blow to Democrats in a key swing state, sparking alarm among the newsletter’s subscribers.

items.subject: Three Days Until the Midterms. How Bad Could It Get for Republicans? (w/ Sarah Longwell) | Bulwark on Sunday
bullets: Sarah Longwell says focus‑group data shows many Trump voters are disillusioned and considering voting Democratic, a trend Bill Kristol says could drive a historic Republican loss in the midterms.

They argue Democrats have unexpected openings in traditionally red states, citing the surprise endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers by Democrat Haley Stevens in Michigan as a sign of shifting alliances.

items.subject: BREAKING: Haley Stevens Endorses Republican in Final Attempt to Tank Abdul El-Sayed
bullets: Democrat Rep. Haley Stevens, after failing to force Senate nominee Abdul El‑Sayed to denounce an anti‑Israel ad, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers two days before the Michigan Senate election, prompting staff resignations and backlash from party leaders.

Stevens had spent $30 million from pro‑Israel lobby AIPAC and was the establishment’s pick, but her fiancé Jason Turkish publicly supported Rogers and appeared with GOP figures, while El‑Sayed barred Stevens from his events.

Party officials, including Michigan Democratic Chair Curtis Hertel and DNC Black Caucus chair Virgie Rollins, condemned Stevens as a “sellout,” calling her endorsement a betrayal of Black voters and the campaign.

items.subject: My decision:
bullets: John Sununu leads New Hampshire Senate polls after GOP pours over $67 million into ads, making the race a potential deciding factor for Senate control.
Incumbent Chris Pappas stresses he has never taken corporate PAC money, framing his campaign as grassroots‑funded and asking supporters for $15 donations to close the fundraising gap.

items.subject: Why 2026 Is a Health Care Election
bullets: Family‑medicine doctor Raymond Rion says Packard Health, a federally qualified health center in Michigan, saw uninsured patients drop from one‑third to one‑tenth after ACA subsidies, enabling expansion but now faces layoffs as Trump‑era cuts to HealthCare.gov subsidies and Medicaid take effect.

Rion warns that rising insurance costs and Medicaid reductions will push more patients to delay care, leading to complications like diabetes‑related organ damage and increased ER visits, straining providers further.
The article argues the 2026 midterms will be a de‑facto health‑care election because voter concern, provider strain, and policy changes make health coverage the pivotal issue.

items.subject: Is the Islamophobic Campaign Against El-Sayed Working?
bullets: Republicans have launched an unusually overtly Islamophobic attack on Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El‑Sayed, with Ted Cruz calling him a “jihadist leprechaun” and ads accusing him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood and wanting to impose sharia law.

The campaign’s extreme bigotry has prompted a focus group of ten Trump‑voting Michigan voters who now disapprove of Trump, revealing mixed feelings about El‑Sayed largely due to distrust fueled by the attack ads.
Despite the hostility, the focus group showed some potential for Democratic gains, indicating the Islamophobic strategy may not fully succeed in swaying anti‑Trump voters.

items.subject: Trumponomics: A Midterm Report Card
bullets: Krugman argues that while overall macro indicators like unemployment and inflation are not disastrous, Trump’s broken promises and rising health‑care costs have left many families feeling betrayed and financially strained.
He claims the economic downturn is uniquely Trump‑driven, citing higher energy prices, stricter immigration enforcement, and tariffs as policy choices that worsened ordinary Americans’ finances.

Krugman promises a detailed midterm report card covering the economy’s shift under Trump, energy, immigration, tariffs, health care, and an overall grade, noting tax cuts and deficits are left for later.

items.subject: A MAGA Blowhard’s $1 MILLION Bet Just Blew Up in His Face
bullets: Clay Travis, a MAGA podcaster, wagered $1 million that oil prices would drop before the midterms, but prices remain high, exposing his flawed predictions.
Tim Miller details Travis’s incorrect claims about Trump’s Iran war and highlights his growing, absurd fascination with Cheesecake Factory.

items.subject: Before bed
bullets: Jon Ossoff, the only Democratic senator up for reelection in a Trump‑won state, urges supporters to donate $10 before midnight to help secure his seat and maintain the Democratic Senate majority.
He frames the race as a defense of the republic against Trump’s alleged power grab, claiming Trump’s actions threaten national security and create fear among Americans.
Ossoff highlights that his 2020 victory not only won a Senate seat but also secured the Democratic majority, positioning the current campaign as a continuation of that effort.

items.subject: Reaching out before tonight’s deadline
bullets: Chris Pappas urges supporters to donate before tonight’s fundraising deadline, warning that New Hampshire’s Senate seat could decide the chamber’s majority.
He notes GOP candidate John Sununu leads polls after $67 million in Republican spending, and claims a few dollars from donors can keep the Granite State blue.

items.subject: Trump Is Everything the Founders Warned About
bullets: Trump’s 2016 election and 2024 return demonstrate a national failure to uphold democratic values, despite his proven unfitness and incitement of the January 6 insurrection.
Over the past two years, Trump has intensified threats to liberty, security, and prosperity, aligning with the dangers the Founders warned against.

items.subject: Alina Habba’s $50 Million Payday Sends Trump Into a Rage
bullets: Alina Habba received a $50 million payment, sparking Trump’s fury and igniting infighting among his allies over how to split the proceeds.
Oil companies are profiting from Trump’s Iran war while American consumers face higher gasoline prices.
Trump has threatened the Federal Reserve and is timing a push to oust Fed Chair Lisa Cook shortly after the midterms.

items.subject: RIP Bill Nordhaus
bullets: Bill Nordhaus, a pioneering economist and Krugman’s mentor, died; he authored the influential 1973 paper "The Allocation of Energy Resources" on exhaustible resource economics.
Krugman recalls working with Nordhaus on that paper, noting his guidance in modeling complex real-world problems and framing economics as a mission beyond a job.
Krugman plans to write a detailed tribute after the midterms, reflecting on Nordhaus’s academic and civic contributions.

items.subject: This Week in Palestine: Settlers Attack U.S. Journalist and Activists as Hebron Lockdown Displaces Thousands
bullets: Israel’s “full lockdown” of the West Bank and ongoing Gaza bombings this week killed at least 15 Palestinians, including a 6‑year‑old girl shot in the neck.
In Hebron, a total closure after two Israeli soldiers were killed led Israeli forces to forcibly displace thousands, demolish homes and give families only minutes to collect belongings.
U.S. journalist Jasper Nathaniel and activist Andrey Kharzhanovsky were arrested after illegal Israeli settlers attacked them during the Hebron lockdown.

items.subject: Final three days
bullets: Today is the last day for early voting in North Carolina, with polls closing at 3 PM before Election Day on November 3rd.
If you haven’t voted or registered, you must vote or register today; registration won’t be available on Election Day.
Volunteers can sign up to help voters in the final days, and a $5 donation will fund last‑minute outreach efforts.

items.subject: Tricks, Tariffs, and Trump’s Corporate Enablers
bullets: The Bulwark’s members‑only live stream on Sunday at 8:30 p.m. ET will feature Tim Miller, Sam Stein, Lauren Egan and others discussing the latest races and taking audience questions.
A post‑midterm gathering, “Ours to Keep: What’s Next for the Republic,” will be held at The Barn Resort near Gettysburg on November 5, with free admission using code gettysburg26.

items.subject: ‘The Day of Accountability Has Arrived’
bullets: Michael Pretti told a Minneapolis press conference that his son Alex was shot dead by federal agents and the DOJ has stone‑walled the family for nine months, refusing to cooperate with a state investigation.

Families of Alex Pretti and Renée Good have filed civil lawsuits against ICE, CBP and senior Trump officials, demanding accountability for the killings and urging political action ahead of the midterms.

Immigration detainee Lucas Santiago Martínez’s case illustrates systemic delays: a waiver that once took 1‑2 years now faces a 53‑month wait, prompting his wife Yesenia to launch a GoFundMe and stress the vote’s impact on detention policies.

items.subject: Jon Ossoff Is Poised to Win Reelection. Is the White House Next?
bullets: Senator Jon Ossoff, backed by a rally appearance with Barack Obama, leads comfortably over Republican Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia’s Senate race, according to recent polls.
Ossoff’s campaign leverages viral clips of his speeches and his mentorship under civil‑rights icon John Lewis, boosting his appeal among young and liberal voters.
Democratic insiders and some Georgia voters see Ossoff’s swing‑state success as a springboard for a potential presidential run.

items.subject: "For all things, including crisis, there should be a season”
bullets: A reader asks Danny Nelson how to support a boyfriend whose chronic anger and cynicism have intensified after a car accident, bike flats, a dangerous job, and his grandfather’s hospice stay, prompting advice on boundaries versus staying in a potentially self‑destructive relationship.

Lila Baer describes her wildland firefighting job—$60K in six months, 16‑hour shifts, sleeping in backcountry camps without showers, building handlines on steep terrain, and the difficulty of hiring and diversity in crews.

Laura Tremaine mourns the sudden death of Rena, the esthetician who waxed her for over twenty years, reflecting on the deep, almost‑friendship loss and the strange grief of losing a long‑term intimate ritual.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Guess What? Polls Can Underestimate Democrats too
bullets: Pfeiffer warns that while recent CNN polls show Democrats leading in several states, historical polling errors in 2016 and 2020 raise concerns about a possible systematic bias.
He notes that midterm polls have been more accurate than presidential ones because they over‑sample super‑voters, but the current blue surge may still be overstated.
Subscriber chat will run all election night for real‑time analysis, encouraging non‑subscribers to join for deeper post‑election breakdowns.

items.subject: $63,989 to go
bullets: The campaign has 16 hours left to hit its $2 million fundraising goal, currently $63,989 short, to fund ads, organizers, and volunteers through Election Day.
Candidate Chris Pappas urges supporters to donate $5‑$25 (or any amount) before midnight, emphasizing that grassroots funding is crucial against John Sununu’s super‑PAC and billionaire backing.

items.subject: Azeem Azhar on the Explosion of Hacking and Other AI Issues
bullets: Azeem Azhar warns that AI models, now as capable as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, can autonomously discover and chain software vulnerabilities, turning the PHP codebase—used by 70% of websites—into a massive attack surface.

He likens this surge to a “Wuhan moment,” where cheap, tireless AI accelerates exploit discovery faster than defenders, exemplified by AI finding severe bugs in software previously tested trillions of times.
The rapid diffusion of open‑source AI models means the same exploit‑finding power spreads quickly, creating a persistent arms race that favors malicious actors who need only a single flaw to succeed.

items.subject: Gating Functions
bullets: US sanctions and a naval blockade forced Venezuela to divert light crude needed as diluent, causing a 25% drop in Orinoco heavy oil output in summer 2021 and a low of 830,000 bpd by December 2025.

After a Delta Force raid captured President Maduro in January 2026, the new government eased sanctions, restored naphtha imports, and production rebounded to 1.25 million bpd, driven by Orinoco and conventional fields.

The episode illustrates how political constraints, not geology, now dominate Venezuelan oil output and highlights the shifting molecular definition of oil as diluent availability becomes a production bottleneck.

items.subject: About Karoline Leavitt
bullets: John Sununu leads in NH polls with $67 million GOP spend, threatening to flip the Senate seat and boost Trump’s agenda; Chris Pappas urges $10‑$15 donations to keep the seat open.

Pappas contrasts his service‑focused record—lower drug costs, veterans’ benefits, small‑biz support, reproductive freedom, Medicare/Social Security—with Karoline Leavitt’s MAGA‑oriented, media‑centric campaign that New Hampshire voters rejected in 2022.
He warns that a GOP win would cement Trump’s Senate control and undermine New Hampshire’s independent, community‑focused politics, urging urgent grassroots funding to preserve the state’s values.

items.subject: BURN MAGA TO THE GROUND
bullets: The Secret Podcast episode features JVL’s complaints, Sarah’s solutions, poll analysis, and a surprise segment, available exclusively to Bulwork+ members.

items.subject: This Week in Democracy – Week 93: Trump Targets El-Sayed, California Voters, and a Familiar Foe Ahead of Midterms
bullets: Trump’s Justice Department charged former FBI Director James Comey with two Espionage Act counts, marking his third indictment in 13 months, while a grand jury declined to indict former aide Cassidy Hutchinson over Jan. 6 testimony.

The administration issued over 100 subpoenas to obtain voting records in at least 13 states, expanded a criminal probe into California voters, and warned all 50 states that election officials could face prosecution for violating federal election laws.

Trump threatened to cancel the Alaska Senate election, called Democratic nominee Mary Peltola a target, and ordered the mass expulsion of more than 150 Afghan immigrants from Louisiana to Pakistan, risking persecution for some.

items.subject: Please
bullets: Senator Jon Ossoff asks recipients to donate $10‑$50 to his 2026 reelection campaign via ActBlue, emphasizing it’s a grassroots effort without corporate PAC or lobbyist money
He frames the contribution as a decisive rebuke to the MAGA movement and a way to protect the future of the Republic

items.subject: What’s Really at Stake in New Hampshire?
bullets: Buttigieg argues that rising living costs in New Hampshire are driven by the Trump‑Vance administration and Governor Kelly Ayotte, urging voters to elect candidates who will lower expenses and block that agenda
He endorses Congressman Chris Pappas for Senate and state candidates Stefany Shaheen, Maggie Goodlander, and Cinde Warmington, noting Pappas’s race will determine Senate control
He urges viewers to watch his recap video, comment, and vote on November 3 to support these candidates

items.subject: Patrick Stewart, R.I.P.
bullets: Patrick Stewart’s 2023 memoir *Making It So* mixes humor with reflections on his Shakespearean roots and iconic roles as Captain Picard and Professor X, underscoring his lasting cultural impact.

Texas denied a $128,000 state film grant to *Elastic Hearts* because it tackled abortion, illustrating how political leaders use arts incentives to enforce ideological compliance, a pattern echoed in other states’ tax‑credit controversies.
The newsletter recommends the darkly comic *Wild Horse Nine*—a Martin McDonagh film starring John Malkovich as a CIA assassin grappling with mortality—as a standout recent release.

items.subject: We Need to Nationalize the AI Companies
bullets: Anthropic proposes a draft AI regulation that would allow a model to cause up to 50 deaths or $1 billion in damage before regulators intervene, arguing these thresholds are “sensible policies” for Congress.

Senior Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger publicly stated a >10% chance that AI could kill all humans within a decade, sparking criticism from former employee Jacob Coxon who warned that AI firms are “gambling with our lives.”
Critics claim such apocalyptic predictions are marketing tactics to inflate an AI bubble, suggesting the industry may be building an extinction‑level threat while also engaging in routine fraud.

items.subject: Stop Whining. Just Win.
bullets: Mary Peltola’s campaign added a second candidate named Dan Sullivan to the Alaska Senate ballot, prompting Republican lawsuits and calls for her removal, though the tactic is legal under Alaska’s ranked‑choice voting system.
Republicans, including national elected officials and President Trump, claim the move is dishonest and demand Peltola be prosecuted or not seated, despite no evidence it violates election law.
The author argues the controversy is a partisan character attack, noting Republicans previously accepted hardball tactics like DeSantis’s gerrymandering, and urges conservatives to stop whining.

items.subject: This Progressive is Vying to Become Florida’s First Black Senator on Tuesday
bullets: Progressive Angie Nixon, endorsed by Barack Obama, is running to become Florida’s first Black senator and the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there since 2012, but polls show her trailing incumbent Republican Ashley Moody by several points.
Nixon’s platform includes Medicare for All, abolishing ICE, and raising the federal minimum wage, while she accuses Moody of sending people to harass her staff and refusing to debate her.

In the interview she addresses mischaracterizations of her Cuba comments, attacks by far‑right activist Laura Loomer, her recent DSA membership, and hints at possibly leaving the Democratic Party after the election.

items.subject: What Texas Trump Voters Really Think of Elon Musk’s Ads
bullets: Elon Musk has spent $190 million on ads supporting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, attacking opponents like James Talarico and a state senator’s husband with claims about gender and Christianity.
Focus groups of 2024 Trump voters who disapprove of Trump’s performance were convened to gauge whether Musk’s spending would help Paxton win a Senate seat.
The newsletter hints that the results of these focus groups will reveal whether the ads are effective, but no definitive outcome is yet reported.

items.subject: From last July to the final weekend
bullets: Since early voting began, Roy Cooper’s campaign and volunteers have contacted over 619,000 North Carolina voters and are urging a final push before the November 3 election.
Tomorrow is the last day for in‑person early voting and same‑day registration in NC; polls open Tuesday 6:30 am‑7:30 pm, with links provided for sites.
The campaign asks supporters to donate $5 to fund final organizing efforts to flip the Senate seat.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: The Top Campaign Issue of the Decade Has Vanished
bullets: The Supreme Court’s 2022 Roe v. Wade reversal has pushed abortion back to state politics, but both parties have largely dropped abortion messaging in 2024 midterms, focusing instead on cost‑of‑living and other culture‑war issues; Democrats cite affordability as a unifying theme, while Republicans avoid rally‑round pro‑life messaging after Trump’s pivot to other issues.

AdImpact and Adsmom data show Democratic abortion ad spend fell four‑fold in 2024 compared to 2022, and abortion ads ranked 15th out of 26 topics in October, below data centers and climate; Republicans likewise have not used abortion as a midterm rallying point, citing a lack of base motivation and a shift toward trans‑rights controversies.

items.subject: A personal note from the campaign trail
bullets: With only four days left, John Sununu leads New Hampshire Senate polls after GOP spends over $67 million on ads and airwaves.
Chris Pappas urges supporters to donate $10‑$15 now to close the gap and keep New Hampshire blue in a race he says could decide the Senate majority.
He emphasizes grassroots outreach across community centers and town events, arguing every door knock and contribution is crucial as the race tightens.

items.subject: Why I Am Thanking Bill and Hillary Clinton Today 🙏🏽
bullets: Bill and Hillary Clinton publicly condemned Republican anti‑Muslim attacks on Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El‑Sayed in Michigan, calling out fear‑mongering and bigotry.

The author criticizes centrist Democrats—Haley Stevens, Josh Gottheimer, John Fetterman, Nancy Pelosi, Chuck Schumer, Kirsten Gillibrand—for remaining silent or even supporting anti‑Muslim rhetoric despite the GOP’s campaign against El‑Sayed.
Midterm stakes are high as the author urges Democrats to match the Clintons’ defense of religious tolerance and reject the GOP’s Islamophobic tactics.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: I Love Election Nights (Yes, Really)
bullets: Dan Pfeiffer says he actually enjoys election nights, viewing them as the payoff for campaign work and a chance to test poll predictions against real results
He offers paid subscribers an election‑night guide, rapid poll‑response analysis, a live Substack chat, a post‑mortem Wednesday piece, and deeper post‑election coverage, with a 20% annual discount
He predicts a strong Democratic showing and hopes Donald Trump faces a decisive defeat

items.subject: Trumpflation and Travel
bullets: A chart of the Fed's preferred inflation gauge shows a sharp rise, marking the last major data point before the midterms.
Krugman attributes the surge to Trump's policies, first tariffs and now war, coining the term 'Trumpflation' for the inflationary impact.

items.subject: Companies That Cozied Up to Trump Brace for a Reckoning
bullets: Corporations that courted Trump—offering gifts, donations, equity stakes, and legal assistance—did so to secure favorable treatment, ignoring constitutional and market rule violations.

With Democrats poised to regain a congressional chamber and wield subpoena power, firms like oil companies face investigations for illegal actions such as facilitating Russian diesel imports under Trump pressure.
Rampell argues that restoring the rule of law will require not only punishing these corporate collaborators but also reshaping incentives to deter future capitulation.

items.subject: Vivek Ramaswamy Pulls His Disturbing Ad After ‘Our Numbers Cratered’
bullets: Ohio GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy halted his controversial “rapist protector mom” ad after internal GOP polling showed his support dramatically fell, prompting calls from party leaders.
The ad, initially defended by Trump and JD Vance, sparked outrage among Ohio Republicans who feared it would damage other GOP candidates on the ticket.
Ramaswamy’s campaign had planned to spend millions on the ad, but staff received relentless pleas from conservatives to pull it, leading to its removal.

items.subject: About our rally with President Obama
bullets: Jon Ossoff says he and President Obama rallied thousands in Atlanta to oppose the Trump administration and his GOP opponent Mike Collins as Georgia voting intensifies
He urges supporters to donate via ActBlue, noting MAGA has spent tens of millions to defeat him but claims they previously won and can do it again

items.subject: Are Never-Trumpers Welcome in the Democratic Party? Mehdi Asks Sarah Longwell
bullets: Sarah Longwell, former Republican operative turned Never‑Trumper, says Kamala Harris’s 2024 campaign failed because centrists saw her as too progressive and progressives saw her as too centrist, leaving her message undefined.

Longwell argues Democrats should consider shifting rightward, cites focus‑group data on former Trump voters abandoning him, and suggests House Democrats prioritize investigating Trump administration officials over impeachment if they regain Congress.

The interview also covers Longwell’s work for a right‑wing lobbyist nicknamed ‘Dr. Evil,’ her view that the GOP helped create Trump, and why she defends Liz Cheney’s alliance with Harris but not progressive figures like Hasan Piker.

items.subject: Your support can’t wait
bullets: With five days left before Election Day, Pappas warns that New Hampshire voters largely vote on that day, making the final stretch decisive for the Senate race.
He notes the GOP candidate John Sununu leads in polls after $66 million of GOP spending, and urges donors to contribute $10‑$15 to close the fundraising gap and keep New Hampshire blue.

items.subject: Mike Rogers May Have an Imaginary Friend Who Loves Tariffs
bullets: Mike Rogers repeatedly tells a fabricated anecdote about a Michigan fabricator adding a second shift due to Trump tariffs, claiming it proves reshoring benefits, despite the story being repeated 31 times over a year and lacking verifiable details.

Rogers updates the anecdote’s timeline and specifics (e.g., industry, number of weeks) each time he repeats it, using it as a rhetorical device to support his tariff‑pro‑policy stance in the Senate race.

items.subject: Inside Trump’s Desperate Final Push to Steal the 2026 Midterms
bullets: Trump and top Republican officials are orchestrating a coordinated campaign to overturn the 2026 midterm results, including false claims of non‑citizen voting, targeting opponents, and threatening Democratic election officials with criminal prosecution.
The Justice Department is allegedly violating its own policies by trying to influence state election administration and arguing courts that the election isn’t legitimate unless Trump wins.

White House officials have not ruled out deploying military, federal law enforcement, or armed ICE agents at polls, a move the author says would be illegal but reflects a last‑ditch escalation to rig the vote.

items.subject: I need your help
bullets: Roy Cooper urges $5 donations to meet a $5 million goal to counter Trump and JD Vance rallies in North Carolina, claiming their presence fuels GOP attacks before the election.
He warns that without sufficient funds, his campaign risks losing the Senate seat to the GOP, citing recent rallies by Trump and Vance alongside opponent Michael Whatley.

items.subject: The Power of Trump Compels Them
bullets: Trump’s influence has reshaped American voters, making a return to pre‑Trump politics unlikely, as shown by PRRI data on shifting attitudes toward Christian nationalism.

Christian nationalism is defined as a nationalist ideology disguised as Christianity, and 48% of Americans view it unfavorably, but support has risen among white non‑evangelical Protestants, white Catholics, and Jews, while falling among Hispanic and black Protestants.

items.subject: Trump Admin Pushes Gender-Swapping Harry Potter Fanfic
bullets: The Trump‑era Department of Education’s X account promoted a gender‑swapped Harry Potter fanfic, depicting Draco Malfoy as a girl, echoing the right’s “Malfoid” meme.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Is This Heaven? No, It’s the Midterms.
bullets: Trump’s fraud narrative is being echoed globally, with Israel’s Netanyahu alleging a stolen election and Brazil’s Flávio Bolsonaro briefly claiming a presidential win before retracting it under Trump’s silence","The Milwaukee Brewers won the World Series despite a small market and modest payroll, while a Hart Research poll shows Louisiana Senate race between Trump‑backed Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis now within 4 points, prompting a last‑minute Trump TeleRally","Pentagon Secretary Pete Hegseth dismissed Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the fifth senior Army officer ousted this year, amid speculation of a renewed Iran war and heightened midterm stakes for controlling U.S. military policy

items.subject: When I walked off the debate stage
bullets: Chris Pappas urges a $15 donation as his New Hampshire Senate race against John Sununu, backed by Donald Trump and $66 million in Republican dark money, nears the final five days before Election Day.
He highlights his stance to protect Social Security and refuses corporate PAC money, framing the contest as pivotal for Democratic control of the Senate.

items.subject: Will the AI Investment Splurge Last?
bullets: A Columbia Business School projection says AI spending will be the largest U.S. investment boom ever as a share of GDP, but Krugman predicts it will stall due to financing limits and borrowing costs rising as lenders grow wary, evidenced by soaring CDS spreads for firms like Coreweave and Oracle.

Public opposition to data centers—majority of Americans oppose new sites and local permits are increasingly denied, with New York imposing a one‑year moratorium and Oracle’s Project Jupiter pipeline repeatedly blocked—adds a political wall to the AI investment surge.

items.subject: 🌻 Dems Are ‘Bleeding’ Team Trump in This Deep-Red State – and Republicans Are Livid
bullets: Republicans fear a disastrous loss in Kansas, where Democrat Adam Hamilton is closing in on Trump‑backed Sen. Roger Marshall, a potential bellwether for a 2026 blue wave despite Trump’s 16‑point 2024 win.

If Kansas flips, GOP insiders expect intense intra‑party blame‑games targeting Trump advisers like Susie Wiles and James Blair, while even a Marshall win may still signal deeper damage to the party’s future.

items.subject: If you’re new here...
bullets: Chris Pappas, a New Hampshire congressman and LGBTQ+ advocate, is running for Senate to fight a system he says favors the wealthy, citing his family’s 109‑year‑old Greek‑immigrant restaurant and 35,000 gallons of homemade ice cream churned annually as proof of hard work and community service.

He highlights his legislative record, including opposing a 2015 bill that would have denied out‑of‑state same‑sex marriages, helping secure civil unions in 2017, and New Hampshire becoming the first state to legalize marriage equality by law in 2019.

Pappas contrasts his bipartisan, results‑oriented approach with Republican opponent John Sununu, accusing the GOP of extreme rhetoric, attacks on reproductive rights, and a Trump administration that prioritizes billionaires over families, while pledging to continue fighting for prescription drug costs, youth engagement, and economic fairness.

items.subject: Trump Keeps Trying to Jail His Enemies. Grand Juries Keep Saying NO
bullets: Trump’s attempts to use grand juries to indict former aide Cassidy Hutchinson and to fire former FBI director James Comey have been rebuffed by a grand jury and a judge, respectively.

Longwell and Weissmann argue the DOJ’s election‑interference investigations in California and Alaska illustrate federal overreach, while highlighting corruption claims against Senator Susan Collins and the lingering Epstein scandal’s impact on Trump.
They conclude that despite these legal setbacks, Trump continues to pursue punitive actions against perceived enemies, underscoring ongoing threats to democratic norms.

items.subject: Why Is the Media Ignoring the New Rape Allegation Against Trump?
bullets: House Judiciary Democrats released a 53‑page report alleging Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein and a new rape claim by a beauty‑pageant contestant, urging an independent special counsel for investigation.
The report cites 11 women, five of whom accuse Trump directly, yet mainstream media largely ignored the allegations, a silence the author argues would not occur for a Democratic president.
The author criticizes CBS News for deleting an unforced error tweet and notes Hasan Piker’s lawsuit against Scott Jennings, but focuses on the media blackout surrounding Trump’s alleged crimes.

items.subject: Republicans Tried to Undercut Black Voters. It’s Blowing Up in Their Faces.
bullets: Republican redistricting after the Supreme Court’s ruling on Section 2 has spurred a surge in black voter turnout, with over 160,000 more ballots cast this year than in 2022, especially in Southern states like Louisiana, South Carolina, and Tennessee’s Shelby County.

Early‑vote data shows a disproportionate rise among younger black voters—contrary to the typical older‑skew of early voting—suggesting heightened political engagement that could flip traditionally Republican districts such as Tennessee’s 5th and 9th and tighten races in Virginia and South Carolina.

items.subject: My day in Georgia
bullets: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto spent a day in Georgia canvassing, meeting Latino voters and volunteers, to boost Jon Ossoff’s tight, must‑win Senate race as Democrats seek to regain control.

She highlighted her role recruiting Ossoff and her 2020 DSCC leadership that helped flip the Senate, urging supporters to donate to both her and Ossoff’s campaigns in the final days before Election Day.

items.subject: Let me explain
bullets: Jon Ossoff urges donors to contribute before his end‑of‑month deadline, warning he’s the only Democratic Georgia senator facing a MAGA‑targeted reelection after Trump’s 2024 win
He says his campaign rejects corporate PACs and lobbyist money, needing a record‑large statewide effort of organizers and voter outreach to win the race

items.subject: How Israel’s Defenders Use Palestinian Voters As Window Dressing
bullets: Deborah Lipstadt praised images of Palestinian citizens voting as proof Israel isn’t racist, while ignoring Netanyahu’s racist ad using the same images and his campaign to intimidate Palestinian voters.

U.S. officials and pro‑Israel groups (Josh Gottheimer, AIPAC, Mike Huckabee) lauded the turnout of ~2 million Arab‑Israeli voters as evidence of Israel’s democracy, yet stayed silent on bans of Palestinian parties and election‑observer intimidation.

Beinart argues this selective praise masks the inherent contradiction of a Jewish state that grants limited franchise to Palestinians in Israel proper while denying voting rights to the 5.5 million Palestinians in the occupied territories, preserving Jewish electoral supremacy.

items.subject: Pre-Election Day Livestream This Sunday Night
bullets: Bulwark+ members are invited to a pre-election livestream on Sunday, Nov 1 at 8:30 p.m. ET featuring Joe Perticone, Andrew Egger, Tim Miller, Sam Stein, Lauren Egan, and Jonathan Cohn.
The panel will discuss the latest developments in the hottest races, take live questions from the audience, and the recording will be posted on the Bulwark Takes feed afterward.

items.subject: Live video with The Bulwark now: Bulwark Book Club: ‘The Age of Acrimony' (w/ JVL & Jon Grinspan) | Mona Charen Show
bullets: Live video now available for paid subscribers: Bulwark Book Club episode on ‘The Age of Acrimony’ featuring JVL and Jon Grinspan on the Mona Charen Show.

items.subject: Trump’s Safe Space for Strongmen
bullets: Flávio Bolsonaro, a Brazilian national accused of laundering over $1 billion, entered the U.S. after a visa was granted by Senator Marco Rubio with the Trump administration’s approval, despite Interpol Red Notice requests.
The case illustrates how the Trump administration’s rhetoric on illegal immigration was contradicted by its facilitation of a high‑profile criminal’s entry into America.
It raises questions about the consistency of U.S. immigration policy and the use of political influence to override legal safeguards.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: NYT Poll: Annie Andrews Can Win South Carolina
bullets: The NYT/Siena poll shows South Carolina Senate candidate Annie Andrews trailing Republican Darline Graham by less than one point with under a week left, a rare near‑tie in a state that hasn't elected a Democrat in 28 years.
Trump’s low approval (42‑55 overall, 38 points below independent baseline) is hurting the GOP ticket, making the race highly competitive and boosting Andrews’ chances.
Republicans are pouring millions into last‑minute ads and Trump is scheduled to rally in the state, underscoring how contested the race has become.

items.subject: Mo Amer and Mehdi Talk Palestine, Comedy, Netflix, and DJ Khaled, LIVE in Houston!
bullets: Mo Amer discusses how the past three years of Gaza genocide have amplified his personal experience by “10,000%,” shaping his Peabody‑winning Netflix series ‘Mo’ which tackles ICE detention, Israeli cultural appropriation, and West Bank oppression

He criticizes fellow Palestinian DJ Khaled for staying silent on the genocide, calling his public persona “off and disconnected,” and reflects on his journey from immigrant Halloween bewilderment to becoming the first Arab‑American to sell out Radio City Music Hall

items.subject: The Case El-Sayed Can Make to Black Voters
bullets: A Michigan Senate attack ad claims Abdul El‑Sayed ignores black voters, citing a 5,000‑word platform with no mention of black issues, but his campaign website lists a 21‑point THRIVE agenda targeting black communities.

The ad is produced by an independent PAC opposing El‑Sayed and is part of a broader misinformation effort in a race where Democrats need strong black voter turnout, a weakness exploited by Republican Mike Rogers.
The controversy highlights deeper tensions between Michigan’s black and Arab communities and debates over progressive versus moderate policy priorities within the Democratic Party.

items.subject: We’ve got to keep our eye on the ball
bullets: Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin now favors Roy Cooper in NC Senate race, but GOP super PACs have spent millions on false claims about his record and Trump & JD Vance are rallying the MAGA base in Greenville and Hendersonville.

Cooper urges grassroots donors to contribute $5 to meet daily fundraising goals, arguing that despite the shift, the GOP remains desperate and any surprise attacks could still jeopardize the seat and Senate control.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: How Do You Solve a Problem Like Elon Musk?
bullets: Elon Musk has poured $446 million into 2024 midterms, with $180 million earmarked for Texas Senate race against James Talarico, using personal attacks on X and direct mail to sway voters.
Talarico’s campaign frames Musk as a shadowy buyer of Texas, claiming Musk’s money fuels Republican candidate Ken Paxton and threatens state resources, echoing past anti‑Soros tactics.

Kristol warns that the rise of nationalism, populism, and authoritarianism worldwide—exemplified by Israel’s split, Hungary’s and Serbia’s politics—signals a return to 19th‑century liberal vs. anti‑liberal struggles, undermining modern liberal democracy.

items.newsletter: Here Be Dragons from Barbara F. Walter
items.subject: What Happens If Democrats Win and Trump Refuses to Accept It?
bullets: Democrats are likely to win the House and possibly the Senate, but Trump may pressure state officials in close races—like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio, Texas, Maine, Michigan—to reject or delay certification, and Republicans could use congressional authority to block seating Democratic members.

Even if Democrats take control, Trump will retain executive power to veto legislation, issue orders, and resist subpoenas, potentially limiting Democratic effectiveness and risking a constitutional crisis, though Congress still holds significant powers such as spending, investigations, and impeachment.

items.subject: Politics is medicine on a large scale
bullets: Rudolf Virchow’s 1848 report linked disease to poverty, arguing that politics—education, jobs, housing, fair taxes, and democracy—is medicine on a large scale; today health policy appears on ballots in at least 29 states and influences federal agencies via the HELP Committee.

Current trends show rising medical debt, measles outbreaks, declining food assistance (lowest in 17 years), and cuts to research funding, underscoring that political decisions, not just pathogens, drive health outcomes.
A 2026 United States of Care survey finds 75% of voters rank health care among top three voting issues and 78% favor a larger government role, making midterm votes directly tied to public health.

items.subject: Netanyahu Collapsed – But Zionists Claim Record Arab Turnout Somehow Absolves Israel
bullets: Israeli turnout hit 77.7%, the highest since 1999, delivering a sharp rebuke to Netanyahu as his bloc fell to 54 seats, 14 short of its previous count.
Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc holds 47 seats, while Arab‑led parties doubled their share to 19 seats, still far from the 61 needed for a governing majority.
Pro‑Israel commentators in the U.S. claim the record Arab turnout somehow absolves Israel, despite the clear electoral setback for Netanyahu.

items.subject: Hack Apocalypse Now
bullets: Critical PHP vulnerabilities uncovered by AI forced European government sites offline, with experts warning a rapid wave of hacks as attackers exploit the flaws before patches spread.

AI‑driven discovery of software bugs is sparking a “Hackening,” likened to the internet’s “Wuhan moment,” and could slash short‑term economic growth as businesses scramble to adopt costly gated‑network solutions.
Regulating AI safety prompts is seen as ineffective because they can be easily reversed, pushing the future toward partially closed digital domains that trade openness for security.

items.subject: Fighting Fascist Crime Families, From Brazil to Israel to the U.S.
bullets: Naomi Klein and Mehdi argue that Brazil’s left‑wing victory, Trump’s backing of Flávio Bolsonaro, and Netanyahu’s grip on Israel show how fascist crime families evade justice while maintaining power.

They note Bolsonaro’s father Jair is jailed for a 2022 coup plot, and Brazil’s prosecution of the coup attempt contrasts with the Bolsonaro family’s corruption, offering a lesson for U.S. Democrats ahead of the midterms.

items.newsletter: Tim, Sarah and JVL - The Bulwark
items.subject: JVL’s Wild 57-Seat Senate Scenario Has Tim Doing the Math
bullets: The hosts warn that Marco Rubio helped Flavio Bolsonaro flee to the U.S. after Brazil’s election loss, while RFK Jr. made overtly racist remarks about Arab voters in Michigan and Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad on Amy Acton sparked further controversy.

They note a Kansas City Star story that Roger Marshall’s hometown is turning against him, Susan Collins is running a elitist ad against Troy Jackson, and Pete Hegseth may eye Marsha Blackburn’s Senate seat as Democrats could achieve a massive wave across the map.

items.subject: Missed goal
bullets: The GOP has spent over $66 million trying to buy the New Hampshire Senate seat, while Chris Pappas refuses corporate PAC money and relies on small donors.
With one week left, Pappas’ fundraising has slumped and he’s setting a 24‑hour $100 K emergency goal to close the gap and fund voter outreach.
He urges supporters to donate $10‑$15 now to help keep New Hampshire blue and flip the Senate.

items.subject: Republicans Warned Vivek Ramaswamy His ‘Rapist Protector’ Ad Was a Terrible Idea
bullets: Multiple Ohio Republicans warned Vivek Ramaswamy that his “rapist protector” attack ad against Democrat Amy Acton would likely backfire, but he ran it anyway, spending millions on promotion.
The ad featured Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about a childhood rape by her husband, a claim based on publicly available court records and prior reporting.
The ad was produced by Ohio firm Strategy Group, which has faced scrutiny for its role in a controversial $220 million DHS advertising contract.

items.subject: Mark Cuban Goes Nuclear on America’s Health Care Giants
bullets: Mark Cuban argues that U.S. health‑care conglomerates artificially raise drug prices, conceal fees, and profit at patients' expense.
He criticizes Democrats' Medicare‑for‑All proposals as misguided and outlines his own strategies to combat price inflation.
Cuban also shares his perspective on the Trump administration's health‑care agenda, suggesting it differs from current partisan narratives.

items.subject: My decision
bullets: Senator Jon Ossoff, the sole Democratic Senate candidate in a Trump‑won state, warns that the president is staging an unprecedented power grab, including freeing Capitol attackers and threatening media outlets.
He claims his 2020 victory flipped a Republican seat and secured the Senate majority, and urges grassroots donations averaging $30 to fund his 2026 reelection campaign.
Ossoff links to an ActBlue donation page, emphasizing that many small contributions are needed to sustain the campaign.

items.subject: Democrats Get Ready for the Sore-Loser-in-Chief
bullets: House Democrats have mobilized nearly 300 staffers to monitor 60‑70 key districts, preparing to document and contest any Republican or federal interference such as ICE presence at polls.
Democratic lawyer Marc Elias warns the Trump administration will employ a “flood‑the‑zone” legal strategy post‑election, but says the party is ready to defeat those lawsuits.
The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit in Alaska over the Dan Sullivan name confusion, seeking to delay certification if the margin is narrow, a move supported by the DSCC and Peltola campaign.

items.subject: Nationalize SpaceX
bullets: The author argues SpaceX poses a national security vulnerability, asserting that private control—whether by Elon Musk or any trillionaire—creates unacceptable risks for America.
He proposes treating “nationalize SpaceX” as a catch‑all term, suggesting options ranging from full nationalization to breakup or aggressive regulation to mitigate those risks.
The newsletter will outline why SpaceX is a danger and then explore possible policy solutions, starting with the claim that the company cannot be trusted to sell combat‑ready fighter jets.

items.subject: The UAE Helped Fuel the Sudan Genocide. Now One of Its Diplomats Wants To Lead the United Nations
bullets: Lana Nusseibeh, former UAE minister and UN representative, is running to become the UN Secretary‑General, potentially becoming the first woman, Muslim, and Palestinian‑descended holder of the post.
She has long denied or downplayed the UAE’s role in the Sudan genocide, a fact that critics argue would undermine UN credibility if she is confirmed.
The Trump administration opposes her candidacy, and many other candidates are believed to be against her, raising concerns about a possible UN leadership misstep.

items.subject: Former Collins Voters Explain Why She’s Tough to Beat—And Has to Go
bullets: Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine, has repeatedly survived tough re-election battles, leveraging her moderate stance and bipartisan appeal to maintain a strong voter base.

In 2020, a group of Mainers who voted for both Joe Biden and Susan Collins revealed that Collins’ ability to win hinges on her willingness to break with party lines on key issues, earning her respect among independents and Democrats.
The newsletter suggests that while Collins remains a formidable incumbent, the political climate is shifting, and her future electoral prospects may face new challenges from both sides of the aisle.

items.subject: Are you with me?
bullets: Governor Josh Stein, Justice Anita Earls, and over a thousand voters attended a Get Out The Vote concert featuring North Carolina artists Davie Circle, Karly Hartzman, Tift Merritt, Hiss Golden Messenger, and Watchhouse x Viv & Riley.
With only seven days to Election Day, the newsletter urges North Carolinians to vote, donate, or volunteer to support a campaign focused on reducing costs and bringing common sense to Washington.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Wave Goodbye to a Republican Congress
bullets: Early voting shows Democrats leading the generic ballot by about 9 points, with Reuters/Ipsos polling Trump at 35% approval and 65% disapproval among registered voters.
Kristol argues the House will almost certainly flip to Democrats and the Senate is very likely to follow, a rare midterm double‑chamber shift last seen in 1994 and 2006.
Egger reports the DOJ filed a third criminal information against James Comey to sidestep a statute‑of‑limitations deadline, but legal experts say it’s procedurally dubious and likely to be dismissed.

items.subject: Bird flu in mink, measles double last year, SNAP at an all time low.
bullets: U.S. measles cases hit 4,588 in 2026—double 2025 and the highest since 1991—driven by a Pennsylvania outbreak with <1% vaccination and spreading to NY, Ohio, Wisconsin, Kentucky, and Indiana.
A Utah mink farm harbored undetected bird flu for two months; mink can mix avian and human flu genes, and officials failed to act, raising pandemic concerns.
SNAP enrollment fell by over 5 million (including 2 million children) to a 17‑year low, threatening free school‑meal eligibility in most states and pushing families toward lunch bills.

items.subject: Donald Trump Is Newly Accused of Rape – and Epstein Allegedly Helped 👀
bullets: A House Judiciary Committee report alleges Donald Trump actively participated in Jeffrey Epstein’s 1990s sexual abuse network, citing five of eleven women who directly accuse him of rape or assault in Epstein‑linked settings such as beauty pageants.
The report claims Trump and Epstein collaborated as “hunting grounds,” using high‑profile events to prey on young women, while Trump denies any wrongdoing.
Zeteo also shares an exclusive Arab‑American poll on the 2028 election, midterms, and Israel‑Palestine issues, plus updates on the Iran war and Israel’s upcoming elections.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: Why Trump’s Rally Tour Is a Gift to Democrats
bullets: Trump’s 2026 midterm approval is the lowest for any president entering a midterm since Harry Truman, yet he’s holding 21 rallies in October, contrary to the usual strategy of unpopular incumbents staying out of the news.

Pfeiffer argues Trump’s rally tour, meant to energize the GOP base, is unlikely to boost turnout and may actually damage Republican prospects by keeping the unpopular president in the spotlight during an election where price concerns dominate.
He notes Trump’s historic strength was mobilizing voters when his name was on the ballot, a dynamic he can’t replicate now, making the rally blitz a strategic misfire that benefits Democrats.

items.subject: Trump Doesn’t Give a Damn About Your Problems
bullets: Trump’s war with Iran has lifted refined gasoline and diesel prices by about $75 per barrel, costing U.S. consumers roughly $560 billion annually, while oil firms profit billions and gave 88% of their 2024 campaign donations to Republicans.
The surge in energy prices, now back to Biden‑era peaks, undermines Trump’s campaign promise to halve fuel costs within a year and fuels Republican poll declines ahead of next Tuesday’s election.

items.subject: Hegseth Needs More T—Poll Shows He’s No Male Role Model
bullets: Only 28% of American adults—and just 18% of 18‑to‑29‑year‑olds—see Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as a strong male role model, placing him second‑worst among nine surveyed public figures, with Trump rated lowest at -18 points; top figures were McConaughey (+33), Obama (+28) and LeBron James (+25).

The poll found 68% of Americans never bet on sports, yet 44% think legalized sports gambling harms sports, and 36% support tighter regulation of prediction markets, with a partisan split favoring more regulation among Harris voters (45%) versus Trump voters (33%).

A majority (51%) oppose transgender athletes competing according to gender identity, while only 31% correctly estimate that fewer than 1% of NCAA athletes are transgender, despite NCAA data showing virtually zero trans participants after recent restrictions.

items.subject: Tough Comp
bullets: The Doomberg newsletter highlights how Russia’s massive missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s energy grid has only recently caused severe damage, underscoring the difficulty of delivering decisive knockout blows from long‑range standoff weapons.

It then notes a Wall Street Journal report that U.S. warships in the Arabian Sea are loading large stocks of standoff land‑attack and bunker‑buster missiles in preparation for potential escalation against Iran, questioning whether such limited assets can achieve a comparable decisive effect.
The author suggests a direct open‑source comparison of Russia‑Ukraine and U.S.-Iran scenarios will reveal stark numbers that make a swift, overwhelming strike against Iran seem implausibly effective.

items.subject: John Sununu’s real record:
bullets: John Sununu, Trump‑endorsed Senate candidate, is accused of lying about a Qatar trip linked to Jeffrey Epstein and of profiting from Wall Street bailouts and Big Pharma after voting against drug‑price cuts.
He allegedly led efforts to privatize Social Security, is backed by dark‑money super PACs with an $800 million war chest, and is portrayed as selling out New Hampshire’s voters.

items.subject: George Conway Is Sickened by What Trump and Vance Have Become
bullets: Conway and Longwell argue Trump’s erratic conduct and broken economic pledges are alienating voters, who feel duped by his promises and personal attacks.
Longwell cites focus‑group data showing Vivek Ramaswamy’s harsh criticism of Michigan health official Amy Acton backfired, deepening GOP’s moral decline.
They claim the GOP’s collapse creates a massive opening for Democrats in the upcoming midterm elections.

items.subject: What It’s Like to Be a Palestinian Citizen of Israel During This Racist Israeli Election
bullets: Palestinian citizens of Israel, 16% of eligible voters, view the 2024 election as existential, fearing that both Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition will continue policies that marginalize them.
The campaign focuses on party blocs, ultra‑Orthodox conscription, and Netanyahu’s fate, but largely ignores how the outcome will affect Palestinians living from the River to the Sea.

items.subject: What happens on October 29th
bullets: The campaign has until October 29 to fund its final TV ads in New Hampshire, needing $500,000 but currently $276,850.87 short with four days left
Opponent and dark‑money groups are spending three times the campaign’s amount, with GOP candidate John Sununu leading polls after $65 million in spending
Because 90% of New Hampshire voters vote on Election Day and there’s no early voting, the final TV push is crucial to reach voters before the deadline

items.subject: A Right-Wing Men’s Club Cracks Up Over Israel—and Trump
bullets: The secretive far‑right Old Glory Club, claiming hundreds of members and 40 chapters, expelled two chapters after a clash over its stance on Trump and Israel, exposing internal fractures.
Critics, including Canada‑based far‑right X user ‘Captive Dreamer,’ mocked the split as evidence that no right‑wing group can stay above the GOP’s ongoing war over ‘groyperism.’
The dispute highlights the club’s paradox: a seemingly whimsical, LARP‑like organization with ominous ambitions to coordinate far‑right men in a governmental collapse.

items.subject: This Congresswoman Says Democrats Should Do ‘Everything’ to Investigate AIPAC
bullets: Rep. Delia Ramirez (D‑Ill.) urges Democrats, if they regain Congress, to investigate AIPAC’s foreign‑agent status after a documentary exposed its influence tactics
Ramirez promotes her bill to block weapons shipments to Israel and ties AIPAC’s role to the 2028 Democratic primary, claiming a pro‑peace, anti‑AIPAC Congress is imminent
She also introduces the ‘Reimaging Safety Act’ to abolish ICE and CBP and replace DHS with a Department of Community Safety

items.subject: Who’s Right? The Polls or the Vibes?
bullets: The author argues that qualitative 'vibes' suggest a massive Democratic wave due to superior candidate quality, poor economic news for Republicans, and President Biden’s extreme unpopularity.
Poll data, however, shows many races still within the margin of error, turning the election into a series of coin flips despite Democratic advantages.
The piece warns of high downside risk for Republicans while warning that the potential Democratic surge could be as dramatic as a 'Hulk Smash Kaiju Tsunami.'

items.subject: Lula’s Incredible Comeback Shows How Democrats Can Win in 2028
bullets: After trailing by 2 million votes in Brazil’s first round, Lula reshuffled his team and hired 41‑year‑old Governor Rafael Fonteles, who introduced an aggressive social‑media strategy and selfie videos for the octogenarian candidate.

Fonteles’ bare‑bones, phone‑held videos focusing on policies like ending the 44‑hour work week and free weekend buses resonated with younger voters, helping Lula close the gap against far‑right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro’s 47% lead.
The author argues Lula’s comeback shows that Democrats can win in 2028 by modernising outreach, using authentic, low‑production content to make voters pay attention to substantive policy messages.

items.subject: This race has changed. Let’s talk about it.
bullets: David Plouffe, former Obama strategist, warned that North Carolina is a must‑win Senate race for Democrats aiming to retake the Senate majority.
Historically tight, the seat was last won by a Democrat in 2008 and by a narrow 10,000‑vote margin in 2016, so complacency could cost it.
Campaign manager Jeff Allen urges donors to contribute immediately, saying the final eight days will focus on voter outreach and organizing to secure the margin.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Trump’s Rallies Have Become What He Covets: Ass
bullets: Trump’s post‑2024 rally tour is marked by exhaustion and repetitive promises, now framed as conditional rewards like $5,000 checks for adults and localized projects that only materialize if Republicans win the midterms, many of which are unlikely or already progressing regardless of election outcomes.

In Serbia, long‑time nationalist leader Aleksandar Vučić was ousted by a student‑driven party, a “tectonic blow” to the Milošević‑era order, while Brazil narrowly re‑elected leftist Lula over Bolsonaro’s son, highlighting a regional shift away from authoritarian incumbents.

items.subject: The Oligarchs Lose a Big One
bullets: Krugman contrasts Meta’s alleged bias with Elon Musk’s overt support for Vladimir Putin, arguing both tech oligarchs influence politics to the right’s advantage

items.subject: Trump: I ‘Don’t Give a Damn’ About Gas Prices – But Obama Knows Voters Do
bullets: Trump told a Georgia rally he’s making "hundreds of billions, trillions of dollars" from oil deals and doesn’t care that gas prices are higher for Americans, citing the Iran war as the cause of higher pump prices.
Obama campaigned in Ohio and Michigan, warning that voters care about gas prices and criticizing Trump’s alleged profiteering, while also mocking Trump’s White House décor choices.
Brazil’s runoff saw Lula defeat Flávio Bolsonaro amid chaos and a delayed concession, and the newsletter notes escalating tensions in the Iran‑Israel conflict ahead of Israel’s election.

items.newsletter: Dan Pfeiffer from The Message Box
items.subject: The Battle for the House Moves into Deep Trump Country
bullets: Democrats are on track for their strongest midterms since 2006, but the focus has been on high‑profile Senate races featuring candidates like James Talarico, Abdul El‑Sayed, Sherrod Brown, Mary Peltola, Roy Cooper, Ken Paxton, Susan Collins and Roger Marshall.

Pfeiffer argues that House races, being more sensitive to the national mood and covering a broader demographic and geographic sample, are a better barometer for future political trends than the limited Senate contests.
He notes the latest shift: the House battle has entered deep Trump‑leaning districts, where Republicans are now scrambling to defend seats that seemed uncompetitive just weeks earlier.

items.subject: South Carolina? Florida? Mississippi?! Democrats Test the Limits of a Blue Wave | Bulwark on Sunday
bullets: Bill Kristol and Lauren Egan analyze whether Democrats can realistically flip Senate seats in traditionally red states Mississippi, South Carolina, and Florida.
They assess the expanding Senate map, highlighting surprising opportunities for Democrats but caution that optimism may outpace the political realities in those deep-red states.

items.subject: A Genocide Was Committed in Sudan’s El Fasher. A Year Later, Survivors Recount the Horrors
bullets: In September 2025, five brothers from the Salman family were killed by an RSF shell in El Fasher’s Tambasi neighborhood during the final weeks of an 18‑month siege that ended with the city’s fall on Oct 26, 2025.

A UN fact‑finding mission concluded the RSF’s mass killings, rapes, torture and enforced disappearances of Zaghawa and Fur civilians in El Fasher constitute a genocidal campaign, with thousands killed.
One year later, families like the Salmans still search for missing relatives, the city remains depopulated, and no RSF perpetrators have been held accountable.

items.subject: What a Blowout Dem Win in ’26 Would Mean for ’28
bullets: If Democrats pull off a sweeping 2026 midterm win—flipping the Senate and winning governorships in traditionally Trump states like Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and Kansas—it would position those states as competitive in the 2028 presidential race, according to Biden‑Harris campaign battleground director Dan Kanninen.
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear echoes this view, arguing that Democratic success in 2026 is crucial for building the momentum and voter perception needed to secure a 2028 presidential victory.

items.subject: Exclusive: AIPAC Whistleblower Speaks to Zeteo
bullets: The hour‑long documentary “Night Flower” investigates AIPAC’s evolution from a one‑man operation to a lobby spending tens of millions on U.S. midterms, featuring former insiders, Rep. Thomas Massie, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio‑Cortez, and a disguised whistleblower questioning whether AIPAC should register as a foreign agent for Israel.

The film, by Pulitzer‑finalist Dion Nissenbaum and Emmy‑winner Zach Goldbaum, argues AIPAC’s influence explains why U.S. policymakers maintain Israel as a close ally despite the Gaza genocide and the costly Iran conflict.
Free Zeteo subscribers can view a 9‑minute preview, while paid subscribers get unrestricted access to the full documentary.

items.subject: GOP Closes Campaign With Unapologetic Bigotry
bullets: Republicans have run a series of anti‑Muslim ads, including a Michigan Senate spot falsely claiming Abdul El‑Sayed wants to impose Sharia law, despite his quote referring only to personal morality.
Similar tactics appear nationwide: AI‑generated ‘Muslims invading’ ad in Georgia, vulgar ‘Allahu Akbar your butt’ remark in Alabama, and Texas GOP’s ‘Don’t Sharia My Texas’ legislation.
The author argues this pattern shows a dangerous, fact‑bending strategy that exploits Islamophobia for political gain, urging voters to demand honesty and reject such bigotry.

items.subject: How Ohio Trump Voters Reacted to Vivek’s Attack Ad
bullets: Vivek Ramaswamy spent $4 million on a Ohio gubernatorial attack ad featuring Amy Acton’s mother, claiming she lied about her past, despite evidence the mother is the liar and hasn’t seen Acton in 48 years.
A focus group of ten Trump‑voting Ohioans, split between prior openness and lukewarm views of Ramaswamy, watched both the attack ad and Acton’s rebuttal featuring her brother to gauge reaction.
The piece argues that understanding such voter responses, even when surprising or infuriating, is essential for protecting American democracy.

items.subject: The Crisis Next Time
bullets: Krugman warns that persistent inflation may force the Fed to sharply raise short‑term rates, risking stagflation.
He cautions that the rapid AI boom could become a bubble whose collapse might trigger a liquidity trap.
Rising long‑term government bond yields raise the specter of a debt crisis, adding to recession risks.

items.subject: Made in Manchester
bullets: Chris Pappas, a lifelong New Hampshire resident and four‑term Democratic House member known for bipartisan work, is now running for Senate with nine days left before the election.

His campaign argues he will fight special interests, protect reproductive freedom, lower costs and curb big‑company pricing, positioning himself as a grassroots alternative to heavily funded Trump‑aligned opponents.
Supporters are urged to donate $25 to fund door‑knocking, voter outreach and ads to help flip the open Senate seat blue.

items.subject: Venues Start Canceling on Vivek Ramaswamy Over His Disgusting Ad: ‘People Don’t Want Him There’
bullets: Vivek Ramaswamy’s Ohio bus tour sparked backlash after his “shameful” ad attacking his Democratic opponent, prompting venue owners to refuse hosting him due to fear of negative publicity and customer complaints.

A top Ohio Republican confirmed that businesses are receiving calls from owners who explicitly do not want Ramaswamy at their events, citing potential angry phone calls, social‑media attacks, and bad press.

items.subject: Elon Musk Has Some Thoughts About The Bulwark. They’re Not Nice.
bullets: Tim Miller rebuts Elon Musk’s threat to The Bulwark, calling Musk’s “live by the sword” comment a dangerous intimidation tactic.

Miller attacks Iowa GOP candidate Joe Mitchell for giving Trump a homemade “Man of the Century” award and for past video showing him ranting about his penis size and making racist remarks toward Black women.
He warns that Rep. Mike Rogers’ support for the Iran war could damage his Michigan Senate bid as voters confront rising gas prices and frustration with Trump’s foreign policy.

items.subject: Can I count on you?
bullets: Republican candidate John Sununu, hand‑picked by Donald Trump, has over $66 million backing to win New Hampshire’s open Senate seat and secure a GOP Senate majority.
